alarmAnalytics.body:
■ What this page is for
Alarm analytics turns the alarms of a period into a statistical report. It helps find problems such as too many alarms, alarms that are too frequent, alarms that nobody handles, or alarms that never recover, instead of looking at alarms one by one. Following the approach of EEMUA 191 (an industry guideline for the design and management of alarm systems), it converts alarm counts into load per operator per 10 minutes, per hour and per day, and measures acknowledgement time, recovery time, floods, chattering, fleeting, consequential and standing alarms. It suits shift engineers doing an alarm rationalization review and managers checking alarm load; the findings are used to adjust rules and never change field configuration directly.

■ What is on the page
1. Filters: start and end time, defaulting to the last 24 hours, with three quick buttons for 24 hours, 7 days and 30 days; the area can be "All areas"; priority is multi-select (Hint, Warning, Critical); rules are multi-select and searchable; Top N can be 5, 10, 20 or 50. Click Query when done.
2. Result context: after a query the start and end time, area and Top N used for this run are shown; if the filters were changed without querying again, a "Filters changed" notice appears.
3. Data range notice: for a long range the earlier part uses pre-aggregated data and the page says from which moment the detail data starts; above the limit it says that only the recent part was analysed.
4. KPI cards: annunciated (total), alarms per operator per 10 minutes with its rating, per operator per hour, per operator per day, peak alarms in 10 minutes, time in flood and flood count, average and median time to ack, average and median time to clear, standing and stale counts, shelved count and hours, suppressed alarms and hours, fleeting alarms and chattering alarms. Ratings are coloured as Acceptable, Manageable, Possibly over-demanding, Likely over-demanding and Unacceptable; the tooltip explains the thresholds.
5. Charts: alarms per 10 minutes as bars (red for floods, with the flood threshold and the acceptable line), alarm trend by priority, priority distribution (the inner ring is the target share) and a Top N bad-actor Pareto chart (bars are counts, the line is the cumulative share).
6. Analysis tabs: Most frequent lists count, annunciated, chatter episodes, fleeting count, share and cumulative share; Chattering lists activations, chatter episodes and max in window; Fleeting lists fleeting count, share and P90 duration; Consequential lists the counts of the two alarms, how often they occur together and the ratio; Floods lists time, duration, count, peak, first-out alarm and main alarm; Standing lists start time, hours and whether acknowledged; Shelving counts occurrences and hours per rule; Rationalization lists type, alarm, suggestion, evidence, current value and suggested value.
7. Drill-down: clicking a chart or a table row opens a drawer on the right listing the matching alarm events with start time, alarm, priority, duration (Ongoing while not cleared), acknowledger and time to ack, and shelved, suppressed or chattering flags, plus the total and the number shown.
8. Export: Excel or PDF, with the analysis start date in the file name. It is unavailable while the filters have changed, when there is no result, and while a query or export is running.
9. Analysis thresholds: only accounts with global configuration permission can see them. You can change operator positions, the acceptable and manageable thresholds per 10 minutes, flood start and end thresholds, chattering count and window, fleeting seconds, standing and stale hours, the consequential window, count and ratio, the frequent alarms per day threshold, target shares and the default Top N. Each item shows its default, defaults can be restored, and saving re-runs the analysis.

■ How to use it
1. Choose the time range and, if needed, the area, priority or rules, then click Query. The page loads the area and rule lists first, then reads statistics and trends.
2. Read the KPI cards first: if per operator per 10 minutes shows Possibly over-demanding or Unacceptable, the load is too high; then check Time in flood and Peak in 10 min to see whether alarms arrive in bursts.
3. Look at Most frequent and the Pareto chart to find the alarms with the highest count and cumulative share; click a table row or a bar to open the details and confirm whether the same tag keeps retriggering.
4. Switch tabs by problem type: chattering points to the recovery deadband or off-delay; fleeting may need an on-delay; consequential may need state-based suppression or merging; standing shows whether the alarm is still valid; shelving shows whether people rely on manual shelving for long periods.
5. Open Rationalization and change thresholds or delays on the alarm rules page as suggested, through the normal approval process. Query again afterwards and compare the KPIs before and after.
6. Click Export Excel or Export PDF when the result must be handed over; confirm first that the filters have not changed.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. "Filters changed, the previous analysis result is still shown": the filters were changed without clicking Query. Export is disabled too; query again before exporting so the report matches the filters.
2. A row of 0 KPI cards or a blank page: there really are no alarms in the selected range and the page shows "No alarms in this range"; the filters may also be too narrow. Widen the range or clear the filters and query again.
3. "Too many detail rows; only the most recent part was analysed": the range is too large and only the recent part is analysed. Shorten the range, or narrow it by area and rules first.
4. Charts and tabs cover only part of the period: for a long range the earlier part uses pre-aggregated data holding only counts and averages, so peak, floods, chattering, consequential and medians cover only the time after the stated moment. Shorten the range when full detail is needed.
5. Saving the thresholds fails: thresholds are global configuration and need global configuration permission; saving sends the version loaded when the dialog was opened, so it may fail if someone else changed them just before. The dialog shows the error; reopen the thresholds dialog and save again. Rationalization suggestions never change any alarm rule automatically.
alarmAnalytics.summary: A health report for alarms: which alarms are most frequent, how fast they are acknowledged, and whether floods occur.
alarmAnalytics.title: Alarm analytics

alarmRules.body:
■ What this page is for
Alarm rules are the criteria for alarms: what counts, which level it gets, whether it needs a delay, and what text is shown. One rule binds to one tag, for example "temperature above 80 raises a warning". This page handles rule maintenance, batch enable and disable, and four-limit generation.
Alarms produced by these rules are handled on the Alarms page, sent out by Alarm notifications and analyzed in Alarm analytics. Users are usually process or instrument engineers and need configuration permission for any area.

■ What is on the page
1. First row: tag filter (shown as "tag name (#id)"); once a tag is ticked, "Selected N" appears with batch enable, disable and delete; Batch four-limit and Add rule are on the right.
2. Second row: a search box filters by tag name or message and splits on spaces; the enabled state offers all states, Enabled and Disabled, and rules being disabled carry Disabling; Clear filters removes the filters; the row also shows "Showing N / M" and Refresh.
3. Rule table: columns tag, type, threshold/level, on-delay and off-delay, conditional suppression, alarm message, enabled and actions, 100 per page. The delay column shows "on-delay s / off-delay s · recovery deadband". The enabled column shows Enabled or Disabled; a disabling rule also gets a yellow Disabling tag whose reason can be read.
4. Row actions: Edit is the primary action; Disable or Restore and Delete stay on the row; Test and Copy are under More. Copy carries the original content and changes the message to "original message_copy".
5. Create/edit dialog: tag, rule type (High-high limit, High limit, Low limit, Low-low limit, State change), threshold, level (Hint, Warning, Critical), on-delay and off-delay (0–3600 s), recovery deadband, conditional suppression, condition tag, alarm message, cause, action and enabled. Defaults are High limit, Warning, 3 s on-delay, 0 s off-delay and enabled.
6. Conditional suppression offers no suppression, suppress while condition tag = 1 and suppress while condition tag = 0 (for example equipment stopped); the last two require a condition tag.
7. Four-limit batch generation: after selecting tags, initial values at 0 %, 10 %, 90 % and 100 % of the range are filled in (editable), then the two level groups, alarm delay, recovery deadband and enable are set. The preview lists only limit types that are not configured yet and the button shows "Create N rules".

■ How to use it
1. Click Add rule and choose a tag; when arriving from the tags page that tag is preselected, and the last saved tag is remembered. Then choose the type and level, enter the threshold (not needed for State change) and set the delays and recovery deadband as required.
2. Set conditional suppression and a condition tag when the alarm should fire only under a condition. The alarm message may stay empty: the system generates it from tag name, value, unit and threshold, or you can customize it with placeholders.
3. Cause says why the alarm occurs and Action says what the field should do; each is at most 200 characters and may be left empty.
4. Click Save; the success message is "Saved". If a required field is missing or the server rejects the rule, a red notice appears at the top and the offending field gets focus.
5. Batch enable or disable: tick configurable rows, click batch enable or disable and the top shows "Enabling N/M"; partial failures open a Batch results dialog listing each row.
6. Four-limit generation: after selecting tags the system skips types that already exist; adjust the limits and levels and click "Create N rules", and success shows "Created N four-limit alarm rules".
7. Verification: filter by that tag and confirm limits, levels and delays; then check on the Alarms page that the alarm fires and recovers.
8. Temporary disable: click Disable, which requires a reason; click Restore to bring it back, or choose Disabling in the state dropdown to review such rules.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. "Please select a tag" or "Please select a suppress condition tag": the tag is empty, or suppression is not "none" but no condition tag is chosen. Complete them before saving.
2. Four-limit generation says "High-high limit must be greater than high limit", "High limit must be greater than low limit" or "Low limit must be greater than low-low limit": the order is invalid or a value is missing. Arrange them from low to high; generation is possible once the message is gone.
3. "All four limit types are already configured for this tag" or "Skipped N existing rules of the same type": the system adds only the missing types; filter the list by tag to check.
4. Tags are missing or buttons are grey: the page decides by configuration permission on the device or area the tag belongs to, and the server checks again.
5. After disabling, active alarms end as disabled, which is why a reason is required for traceability; after restoring, alarms are judged by the current value.
alarmRules.summary: Tell the system what counts as an alarm, which level it is, and whether it needs a delay.
alarmRules.title: Alarm rules

alarms.body:
■ What this page is for
The Alarms page is where field alarms are handled. An alarm is a device asking for help; this page separates alarms that are still active, alarms that have recovered and alarms that nobody has acknowledged yet, and it can shelve rules that should not remind for a while. It suits operators acknowledging alarms day to day, shift engineers clearing alarm floods and managers checking history. An alarm flood banner appears at the top of the page; the list shows only "All active" by default, meaning alarms that are not cleared, not shelved and not suppressed, so the first screen is not filled with recovered alarms waiting for acknowledgement.

■ What is on the page
1. Three tabs: Live alarms shows alarms that are active or waiting for acknowledgement; Shelved shows the shelved rules and their reasons, and the number in brackets is the shelved rule count; Alarm history queries past records by time range.
2. State filters: All active, Active and awaiting acknowledgment, Active unacknowledged, Returned awaiting acknowledgment, Active acknowledged, Shelved and Suppress, each with a count. The active unacknowledged count is red and returned-awaiting count is orange. The far right shows how many rules are disabling.
3. Query fields: level can be All levels, Hint, Warning or Critical; keywords filter by alarm content; the live tab also offers priority-first or newest-first sorting. The history tab adds a time range of the last 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours or 7 days, or custom start and end times; click Query after changing anything.
4. Actions: with acknowledge permission the live tab shows Ack selected and Ack visible with the acknowledgable count in brackets, plus Silence horn and Refresh. Ack visible applies only to acknowledgable records on the current page that match the filters.
5. Alarm list: each row shows state (Unacknowledged, Returned unacknowledged, Confirmed, Cleared acknowledged and so on) and level, and may carry First out, Shelved, Suppressed and Chattering flags below. First out is the earliest alarm of a flood episode and is usually the root cause; the tooltip of a suppression flag gives the reason or says Conditional suppression. Under the alarm text the source (device / tag) is shown, and alarms with a gateway also show Gateway #id.
6. Other columns: value, start time and duration, end time and reason (Ongoing while not cleared), acknowledger and acknowledgement time. Rows that are critical, still active and not shelved are highlighted.
7. Action column: Acknowledge is the only primary action, and it appears for unacknowledged rows when permitted. Add note, Shelve, Unshelve, Open screen and Records are under that row's More: Add note when permitted; Shelve while the rule alarm has not ended; Unshelve when already shelved; Open screen when the alarm has a tag; Records is open to everyone and shows the handling timeline, cause and suggested action, and the number of outgoing notifications.
8. Batch acknowledgement result: the top shows how many succeeded, failed and were skipped after a state change, with the failure reasons; failures can be retried with "Retry failures in the current list".
9. History tab: shows "Queried: start to end" and the total; 50, 100, 200 or 500 per page. Above 5000 matches only the first 5000 can be browsed, with a hint to narrow the range.
10. Shelved tab: columns rule ID, tag ID, reason, operator, start time, expiry time and actions; anyone with acknowledge permission can Unshelve directly here.

■ How to use it
1. Daily acknowledgement: stay on Live alarms and All active and look at severity first. Find the alarm and click Acknowledge; a note is optional, submitting shows "Confirmed" and the record becomes confirmed.
2. Batch handling: tick the unacknowledged rows you may acknowledge, click Ack selected, check the count in the confirmation and submit. Progress shows "Acknowledging completed/total"; check the result and expand the reasons of any failure, then retry.
3. Shelving a nuisance alarm: open that row's More, then click Shelve, choose a duration from 15 minutes to 8 hours and enter a mandatory reason (for example "instrument calibration in progress"); submitting shows "Shelved". Shelving applies per rule and lifts automatically on expiry; unshelving also asks for confirmation, because new alarms from that rule will notify again.
4. Add a note: open that row's More, then click Add note; the content is required (at most 1000 characters) and saving shows "Note saved". A note does not acknowledge the alarm.
5. History: switch to Alarm history, choose a preset period or custom start and end times and click Query. If the time was changed without querying, the page says it still shows the previous result. Records found there can also be acknowledged; Add note, Shelve and Records are under that row's More.
6. Silence horn: click Silence horn; the system lists only panels you may acknowledge and silences them one by one after a second confirmation. It only stops the field sound: it does not acknowledge alarms and does not change the browser sound switch.
7. Entering from other pages: when the URL carries a state or tag the filter is applied automatically; the tag filter appears as a removable chip and clicking close removes it.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. Batch acknowledgement reports "skipped after a state change": the selected alarms were acknowledged or cleared by someone else while you were working, and the system skips them instead of failing the whole batch. Check the skipped count and refresh and select again if needed.
2. The Shelve submit button is grey: the reason is empty. Shelving requires a reason of at most 500 characters; when the server rejects it the error appears next to the reason field.
3. History says "More than 5000 matches": the range is too large and only the first 5000 rows can be browsed. Narrow the range, or filter by level, keyword or tag and query again.
4. "Time range changed, the previous query result is still shown": the time was changed without clicking Query. Only Query reads the new range; on the live tab level, keyword, state and sorting changes refresh automatically, on the history tab they do not.
5. Some alarms cannot be acknowledged or have no button: acknowledgement permission is decided by the area the alarm belongs to; without permission for that area the button is not shown and the server checks again. Accounts without access to the Alarms page cannot enter from other pages either.
alarms.summary: The alarm workbench: see what is unacknowledged, what has recovered, and what is temporarily shelved.
alarms.title: Alarms

annunciators.body:
■ What this page is for
Annunciator connects alarms to field hardware: horns, sounders or three-colour stack lights. When an alarm occurs the system writes the configured output tags to their active value so people on the shop floor notice even without watching a screen; when the state falls back it writes the inactive value. This page covers panel configuration and manual operation: creating panels, binding output tags, silencing, testing and deleting.
It does not decide alarms; Alarm rules do that, and this page is driven by them. Silence horn on the Alarms page is another entry point, and both only affect sound and light, which is not the same as acknowledging an alarm. Configuring panels needs area configuration permission, silencing and testing need alarm acknowledge permission, and the front end hides buttons by permission while the server checks again.

■ What is on the page
1. The header explains "Horn/stack light outputs and browser sound"; Refresh and New panel are on the right, the latter only with configuration permission.
2. Panel table: name, area, enabled, mode, outputs, state and actions. An empty area shows Global; the mode shows Latch or Follow and decides how the output falls back when the alarm disappears, so choose it by the field wiring convention; outputs is the number of bound outputs.
3. State column: silenced panels show grey "Silenced"; otherwise the current driving level (Hint, Warning, Critical) is shown, "Idle" when nothing drives it, plus " · Horn on" while the horn is sounding.
4. Row actions: Silence, Clear silence (only while silenced), Test, Edit, Delete. Silence and Test require alarm acknowledge permission for the panel area; Edit and Delete require configuration permission, and global panels require global configuration permission. Deleting asks "Delete this annunciator panel?".
5. Create/edit dialog: name, area, enabled, mode (Follow or Latch), silence minutes (1–120), browser sound and outputs. Each output can be Horn, Beacon, TowerRed, TowerYellow, TowerBlue or TowerGreen (the red, yellow, blue and green lamps of a stack light), then choose the output tag, enter the active and inactive values, and use Add output or delete a row.
6. The output tag dropdown lists writable tags only, without calculated or derived tags, and requires configuration permission on the device the tag belongs to.
7. When creating, an account with global configuration permission defaults to Global; otherwise the first configurable area is preselected, so missing permission is not discovered only on save.

■ How to use it
1. Click New panel and enter a name; an empty area means global, but only global configuration permission can choose that.
2. Choose the mode: Follow suits outputs that change with the alarm state, Latch suits outputs that need manual silencing before reset; decide by field wiring and process requirements.
3. Set the silence minutes and the browser sound.
4. Click Add output, choose the type and a writable tag (writable and not calculated or derived), and enter the active value (written while an alarm drives it) and the inactive value (written on fallback), commonly 1 and 0. One panel can carry several outputs, such as a horn plus a red lamp.
5. Click Save; "Saved" appears, the list refreshes and shows the current state.
6. Verification: click Test, "Test triggered" appears; confirm that the field horn or stack light operates. Test only exercises the hardware channel and does not change alarms.
7. Click Silence when it must be quiet during an alarm; "Silenced" appears; click Clear silence to restore.
8. Click Delete and confirm when the panel is no longer needed.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. The output tag dropdown is empty: only writable, non-calculated, non-derived tags are allowed, and configuration permission on the device the tag belongs to is required. Check writability and area ownership on the tags and devices pages first.
2. Global cannot be selected when creating: the account lacks global configuration permission; ask an administrator to create global panels, otherwise saving is rejected.
3. New panel, Edit or Delete is not visible: buttons are hidden by permission. Creating needs configuration permission on any area, editing and deleting need permission on the panel area, and global panels need global permission.
4. Silencing works but Clear silence is missing: that button appears only while the state is Silenced. If the state did not change, the silence request did not succeed or the page is not refreshed; click Refresh and look again.
5. The state stays Idle and Test does nothing: check that the panel is enabled and that the output tag address and active value match the wiring logic; if a level is shown but nothing operates, it is usually a wiring or module problem.
annunciators.summary: Connect alarms to physical horns and stack lights so the shop floor can hear and see them.
annunciators.title: Annunciator

assets.body:
■ What this page is for
Device assets answers three questions: what equipment do we have, what was repaired, and do we have enough spares. The ledger keeps each asset's code, model, area and warranty; work orders track a job from report to completion with the resolution and downtime on file; spare parts stock moves with every issue. Built for maintenance teams and storekeepers. The page does not auto-refresh — “Refresh” reloads all three tabs at once.

■ What is on the page
1. Three tabs: Asset ledger, Work orders and Spare parts, each with its own search and filters.
2. Asset ledger: search by code, name, model or location; filter by status and area. Statuses: In service, Standby, Maintenance, Retired. “Linked acquisition device” ties an asset to a device; picking a device fills in its area.
3. Work orders: numbers are generated automatically; types are Corrective, Preventive, Inspection and Improvement; priorities Low to Urgent. Row actions follow the status: Start, Hold, Resume, Complete, Cancel order.
4. Parts used: “Parts used” on an order shows issued parts and issues more, deducting stock immediately; completed or cancelled orders cannot issue parts.
5. Spare parts: stock below the minimum is flagged “Low stock” in red, with a “Low stock only” filter. Stock in, Stock out and Count movements are logged with balance, operator and linked order under “Movements”.
6. Permissions: adding, editing and deleting assets and parts needs Configure; creating orders, status changes, issuing and stock movements need Control — both per area. Buttons you cannot use are hidden.

■ How to use it
1. Register assets: “Add asset” on the ledger tab; fill in code and name, pick an area. Linking a device sets the area automatically; changing the area clears a mismatched device.
2. Report a job: “New work order” on the work orders tab; pick the asset (area and device follow), type, priority and assignee. The number is automatic.
3. Work the order: “Start” moves it to In progress; “Hold” and “Resume” pause and continue; “Complete” requires a resolution and the actual downtime in minutes (0 means no downtime).
4. Issue parts: “Parts used” on the order row, pick a part and quantity, then “Issue” — stock deducts and the movement is logged. Stock out from the parts tab can also link an order.
5. Replenish stock: “Stock in” with a quantity; use “Count” when the book stock is wrong — the balance is set directly to the counted quantity.
6. Audit: “Movements” on a part lists every move with balance, operator, time and linked order.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. Deletes are guarded: an asset with open work orders, or a part with movements, cannot be deleted. Disable it instead — disabled parts cannot be issued.
2. Only Open or Cancelled orders can be deleted; completed or cancelled orders can no longer be edited or change status, so cancel with care.
3. Completing an order requires a resolution; the save is rejected without one.
4. Low stock means stock < minimum stock; set a minimum when creating a part or it will never be flagged.
5. Search runs on Enter or clear; filter dropdowns apply immediately. “Enabled only” hides disabled items.
6. Missing buttons usually mean your account lacks Configure or Control on that area — ask an administrator to adjust area grants.
assets.summary: One place for the asset ledger, maintenance work orders and spare parts — every repair and part issue leaves a trail.
assets.title: Device assets

calcJobs.body:
■ What this page is for
Calculation jobs handle long-running calculations that go beyond a single calculated tag: totalling consumption from pulse water or energy meters; accumulating equipment running hours while an input is above a threshold and flagging due maintenance; integrating instantaneous power into energy and splitting it into peak, high, flat and valley bands; or writing multi-step logic in a restricted script or a C# script. Jobs run on the server and write their results to derived tags named job.output, which can be used in trends, alarms, reports and screens like ordinary tags. The value before a reset is kept in a snapshot for checking.

■ What is on the page
1. Toolbar: search by name or type, a refresh-every-3-seconds switch, Refresh and New calculation job. The create button appears only with area configuration permission.
2. List: job ID and name (with type, area and version), inputs / cycle (input tags, or readable and writable tags for script jobs, with enabled state, cycle and reset mode), current result (output name, value and derived tag ID, with a red tag when maintenance is due), cycle / hints (current cycle number, a running tag, the latest error or event, script steps and elapsed time) and actions.
3. Actions: Edit, Snapshot, Reset, Acknowledge unknown commands, Maintenance done, Delete. Reset appears only for non-script jobs and Maintenance done only for running hour jobs.
4. Edit dialog: name (at most 80 characters), type (cannot be changed when editing), area, enabled and cycle. Counters have input type, pulse weight, counter full scale and maximum increment; running hour jobs have a running threshold and a maintenance threshold; energy integration has a power tag and time bands; script jobs have readable tags, writable tags, input validity, output unit and script.
5. Snapshot dialog: reset time, reason, cycle and the value before the reset; it says no snapshot when none is recorded.

■ How to use it
1. Create a job: click New calculation job, choose the type and area, enter the name and cycle, then choose the input tag. Pulse count needs the pulse weight; flow integration needs a conversion factor that converts the flow unit to per second, for example about 0.000277778 for cubic metres per hour. Full scale handles counter wrap-around; leave the maximum increment empty for no limit.
2. Running hour jobs: enter the running state tag and the running threshold; an input above the threshold counts as running. Enter the maintenance threshold, and the list shows Maintenance due once it is reached.
3. Energy integration: enter the power tag and add peak, high, flat and valley start and end times one by one in the time bands. A start later than the end means it crosses midnight; time not covered counts as flat.
4. Script jobs: enter readable and writable tags as IDs separated by commas. A restricted script writes one $variable = expression, @output = expression or #id = expression per line and can use $dt, $hour, $minute, $weekday, $day and $month. The type list does not offer Restricted script when creating; existing jobs keep that type when edited. For C# advanced scripts first confirm that the server has it enabled, then compile or preview (nothing is dispatched) and review diagnostics, output, intended writes and logs; preview never writes to the field.
5. After saving, the list updates the result every cycle. Reset at the zero point; click Maintenance done after servicing.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. Saving asks to choose an area you may configure: the selected area is outside your permissions or no area is available. Ask an administrator for access and retry.
2. The Save button of a C# script is grey and says the C# Worker is disabled: the server capability is not open, this is not a syntax problem, and permissions and isolation must be configured first.
3. An Acknowledge unknown commands button appears: the previous write result is uncertain, and the button can be clicked only while the job is not running. Verify the field device and the command audit records first; after acknowledgement the previous target value is kept without resending, and only a future target value change is sent again.
4. Bad input quality skips the whole run for script jobs: the current result stops and the latest error is shown. Check input quality and validity instead of shortening the cycle.
5. Deleting a job also deletes its derived tags and snapshots: the confirmation dialog names the job. To stop calculating only, use the enabled switch in the editor.
6. Closing or leaving with unsaved changes asks whether to discard them, and a browser refresh asks as well.
calcJobs.summary: Handle more complex background work such as pulse counting, flow integration and advanced scripts.
calcJobs.title: Calculation jobs

calculations.body:
■ What this page is for
Calculated tags compute a new tag from the values of existing tags without extra sensors. For example two temperatures can be averaged into one tag, inlet and outlet temperatures subtracted into a difference, or output divided by time into a rate. Calculation runs in the centre and the result has a current value, quality and history like an ordinary tag, so it can be bound to screens, used in alarms and reported. Use it when a new metric is needed and changing the PLC program is not convenient. Input tags must exist in tag configuration first; a saved calculated tag also appears in the tag list with the expression in the address column. Entering this page requires configuration permission on any area.

■ What is on the page
1. Toolbar: search by name, expression or ID; a refresh-every-2-seconds switch; Refresh calculation status; New calculated tag.
2. List: tag ID and name (with unit and version), expression / inputs (the expression text and the referenced IDs, or a constant expression when nothing is referenced), run settings (enabled or disabled, calculation cycle, input validity), current value / quality (Not refreshed yet when the data has not updated for more than 5 seconds), time / hints (the last calculation time or waiting for calculation, plus definition errors or current errors) and actions.
3. Edit dialog: name (required, at most 100 characters), enabled, description, area, insert tag reference, calculation expression (required, at most 4096 characters), calculation cycle, input validity, unit, storage mode, history deadband and storage cycle.
4. Dialog footer: Reload definition, Cancel, Validate and preview and Save calculation. Syntax help sits under the expression.

■ How to use it
1. Click New calculated tag and enter a name. An empty area follows the area of the input tags, and only global configuration permission can clear it; area configuration accounts can choose only from their own areas.
2. In the Insert tag reference dropdown find the input tag by name or ID, click insert to append #id to the expression, then add operators and brackets. Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, comparison, &&, ||, if, min, max, abs, sqrt, pow, clamp and round are supported; boolean results are 1 or 0; no file, network or system code can be written.
3. Click Validate and preview. The system evaluates once with the current input values; it does not publish, archive or raise alarms. The result shows the preview value, quality and referenced IDs, and a failure says the trial calculation failed. The preview is cleared when the form changes and must be run again.
4. Set the calculation cycle (100–600000 ms), input validity (100–3600000 ms), unit and storage mode. Change storage needs a history deadband; periodic storage also needs a storage cycle greater than 0.
5. Click Save calculation. A success message appears and the list refreshes; the new tag starts updating on its cycle in realtime monitoring or tag configuration.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. An input older than its validity is not silently replaced by the old value: the quality is no longer Good or the current value stops. Check the input device acquisition first, then consider the validity; do not raise it without limit just to get a number.
2. "Please fill in the name and expression": the name or expression is empty; complete it before saving.
3. "The calculation definition was deleted, review the configuration and close the editor": someone deleted the definition while you were editing. Close the dialog, refresh the list and create it again.
4. "Discard the unsaved calculation definition" when cancelling or leaving: the form has changes. Keep editing, or discard and lose this change.
5. Deleting is refused when there are calculation dependencies: other calculated tags, alarm rules or screens still reference it. Remove the references or disable the rules first; history is kept.
6. The preview reflects only the current set of inputs, not every future cycle; after changing the expression, preview again before saving.
calculations.summary: Create new tags from existing values with a formula, such as efficiency, difference or average.
calculations.title: Calculated tags

console.body:
■ What this page is for
The runtime workbench assembles several process screens into one operator interface. Operators can watch several areas in one window without switching pages, and the most severe alarms are pinned at the top so urgent problems are handled first. Layouts are usually arranged and published by a configuration administrator in workstation configuration, and operators only use them; when no layout is specified, the published layout assigned to the local workstation is preferred. Multi-monitor industrial PCs can open separate windows on each monitor and place them on the field displays.

■ What is on the page
1. The top bar always shows the layout name, the version (a quiet outline for a published version, a warning color for draft preview), monitor buttons when there is more than one monitor, the workstation label (the workstation name when control is allowed, and a warning color plus the monitor-only suffix when it is not), More and this page guide. Layout switching, Open into, Monitor only, Refresh, Open every display, Configure workbench (shown with global configuration permission), Open on each monitor, Fullscreen and Back are inside More: click More once to open the panel, and click More again or outside the panel to close it.
2. Alarm banner: level, state (Active · unacknowledged, Active · confirmed, Returned · awaiting acknowledgment), text and start time of the most severe alarm; the right side shows "Unacknowledged X / active Y" and "awaiting acknowledgment Z"; above 200 alarms a hint says only the 200 highest-severity alarms are listed; when alarm data has not updated for more than 10 seconds the page says the alarm details need verification.
3. Layout regions: process screens, alarm lists or the screen directory arranged on the configured grid. The alarm list shows level, state, start time, text and an action column (Acknowledge, Confirmed or not acknowledgeable), with View all alarms in the top right; picking a screen in the directory opens it in the current target region.
4. Status notices: when a newly published layout version is found, a notice with the new version and an action to apply it appears; there are also time notes such as "Alarm details updated: ...; summary updated: ..."; failures to read the screen directory, validate the layout version, acknowledge an alarm or open a window are each reported separately.
5. Empty state: with no runnable layout the page says no published console layout can run, explains that publishing screens does not mean a workbench is configured, and offers shortcuts to create a workbench, configure the local workstation, run a single screen and retry (when permitted).

■ How to use it
1. Open the runtime workbench. Without a specified layout, a registered local workstation uses its assignment, otherwise the first available published layout is used.
2. On multiple monitors, switch the current window with the monitor buttons on the top bar. To choose which region a screen opens into, open More, pick the target region in Open into, then click a screen in the screen directory.
3. Read the alarm banner at the top first and handle the most severe entry; to acknowledge, go to the alarm list and click Acknowledge; without permission the list shows not acknowledgeable.
4. When a new layout version is announced, apply it and confirm; region navigation resets and floating panels close, and the version number at the top should change.
5. For large displays, open More and turn on Monitor only, which disables control actions. Fullscreen and Back are in the same More panel.
6. To watch on several physical screens, open More and click Open on each monitor, choose the physical monitor or "a normal new window (not positioned)" for each logical monitor in the monitor mapping, then click Open; when several logical monitors map to the same physical screen the page warns about overlapping windows.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. "No published console layout can run": the layout is not published, or the account lacks configuration permission; with permission create a workbench quickly, otherwise contact an administrator.
2. "The local workstation has no published layout assigned" or "The specified runtime layout does not exist or is not published": the local registration is invalid, the assignment is empty, or the layout was deleted or unpublished. Register and assign again in workstation configuration, or choose another published layout from the layout list inside More.
3. The alarm count shows "--" or says the alarm summary needs verification: the alarm interface failed, or the data has not updated for more than 10 seconds. Click Refresh inside More; if it keeps failing, check the service connection and the data on the Alarms page.
4. Clicking Acknowledge reports a failure: the account lacks permission for the alarm area, or the alarm is already acknowledged or has recovered. Showing Confirmed or not acknowledgeable is normal; do not click again.
5. Monitor only is inside More and affects this browser only and changes neither account permissions nor workstation configuration; when the workstation has control disabled, the server still refuses control even if the switch is on here.
console.summary: The operator runtime: several screens in one window, with the most important alarm at the top.
console.title: Runtime workbench

control.body:
■ What this page is for
Field control is the dispatch desk for control actions. One dispatch passes through control ownership (local/remote), tag-out, limits and rate of change, permissive/interlock, operator confirmation, dual approval, write and read-back, and independent feedback, all by area permission and fully audited. Operators approve pending recipe downloads, sequence runs and tag-outs here, shift supervisors judge whether a request may proceed, and configuration administrators set up control policies, sequences and writable tags. Writes from realtime monitoring and process screens are checked against the policies here, and recipe downloads and sequences that need approval also appear under Pending approval. Entering this page requires control permission on at least one area.

■ What is on the page
1. A hint icon sits next to "Operation rules" at the top and Refresh on the right; load failures, pending approval list failures, run record failures, area list failures, mode read failures and operation failures appear as red notices.
2. Pending approval tab: the label carries the pending count; columns content (a write shows "tag <- target value", a recipe shows "name v version" with parameter target values, a sequence shows "Sequence: name"), requester, validity (shown only while pending and red below 60 seconds), state (Pending approval / Executed / Failed / Rejected / Timed out / Withdrawn), result and actions. Requests from others show Approve execution and Reject, your own show Withdraw only; all open a confirmation with the request summary and remaining validity, and accept a review comment.
3. Tag out tab: choose the object (grouped by device and tag) and the tag type (Do not operate / Maintenance), enter a reason (at most 200 characters) and click Tag out; tick Show removed tag-outs to see history. The table lists object, tag, reason, placed and removed.
4. Control mode tab: columns device, mode (Local/Remote, shown as pending verification when reading fails), last switch (person · time · reason) and actions; in Local the centre, screens, sequences and scripts cannot write.
5. Sequences tab: New sequence at the top; the table lists name, step summary, approval (Dual when two people are required) and Run/Edit/Delete. Run records below list run, state (Running/Done/Failed/Aborted), steps (state, count, message), execution (started by, approved by, time), flow chart and abort.
6. Sequence editor: name (at most 100 characters), area, dual approval required before execution, description (at most 500 characters); editing is available in the flow chart or the table, with validation results shown live in the top right; step types are write tag, wait, condition branch, parallel, join, jump/loop and end, with write value, completion condition, true -> / false ->, branch and join, join mode, target and maximum count (1–1000), next step, timeout (100–600000 ms) and failure handling.
7. Control policies: select a writable tag and click Configure to list the policy summary with Edit and Delete. The dialog has operator confirmation (API requests must carry the confirmation marker), dual approval with validity (30–3600 s), operation limits, maximum change per write, permissive/interlock conditions, a message shown when they are not met (at most 200 characters), feedback conditions and timeout (100–600000 ms); tags without a policy get basic checks only.

■ How to use it
1. Pending approval: check the content and remaining validity, verify the field value in realtime monitoring if needed, then click Approve execution or Reject and write a review comment. The state then becomes Executed, Rejected or Timed out; for sequences the run ID is shown and the run records can be checked.
2. Tag out: choose the object and tag type, write the reason and click Tag out; success is confirmed by a "Tagged out" message and a new row. When maintenance ends click Remove tag-out with a note; only the person who placed the tag or someone with configuration permission for that area can remove it.
3. Switching control mode: click Switch to Local/Remote, enter a reason and confirm; "Switched" and a changed label mean it took effect. Switching back to Remote always requires a reason.
4. New sequence: click New sequence, enter name, area and description, choose the editing mode, click Add step and fill in the properties on the right; save once the top right says validation passed. To run, click Run; the confirmation lists every step; success shows "Run #id started", or "Submitted for dual approval" when approval is required. Open the flow chart during a run to see each step state and Abort if needed.
5. Control policies: select a tag and click Configure, switch on operator confirmation and dual approval as needed (dual approval needs a validity), set limits, maximum change per write, permissive conditions and feedback conditions, and click Save; "Saved" and the tag appearing in the list complete the setup.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. New sequence, Edit and Delete are missing or a policy cannot be changed: usually the account lacks configuration permission for that area; running, tagging out and switching control mode need control permission. Ask an administrator to grant permission by area.
2. A write is rejected after tagging out: a Do not operate tag blocks everyone; a Maintenance tag allows only the person who placed it, and removal needs that person or the area configuration administrator with a note.
3. After approving, "The request has expired or was already handled, refresh the list and check", or the state becomes Timed out: the request was handled by someone else or passed its validity. Refresh and work from the latest state; do not approve again.
4. Saving a sequence fails: common causes are a duplicate ID, unreachable steps, a parallel branch that does not join at the same step, or a jump loop without a maximum count. Fix each item following the validation hints.
5. Control mode shows pending verification: the mode was not read, so the switch button is unavailable; click Refresh and retry, and the tab header shows the actual error.
control.summary: Manage approvals, equipment locks, local/remote mode, sequences and control policies in one place.
control.title: Field control

devices.body:
■ What this page is for
Device configuration is the address book of the collection system: it records the protocol, address, collection cycle and area of every PLC and instrument. The collection service connects devices according to these entries; if a device is not registered or the protocol and address are wrong, no data appears in realtime monitoring. New lines, replaced PLCs and offline device troubleshooting are handled here. After saving a device you still need tags on the tag configuration page and thresholds in alarm rules; the three together make it complete. Entering this page requires configuration permission on any area.

■ What is on the page
1. Filter bar: the search box accepts device name, host, serial port, endpoint, area or protocol name; the protocol dropdown is built from the loaded devices; the enabled state offers all states, Enabled and Disabled. Click Query or press Enter after changing anything, otherwise the page says the previous result is still shown. Clear filters restores everything at once; the result count and Refresh sit on the right.
2. Engineering columns switch: turning it on adds ID, collection site, station number, byte order, collection cycle and timeout columns; collection site shows Gateway #id or Center (local).
3. List: name (with a View tags link below), area, protocol, address (OPC UA shows the endpoint URL, serial protocols show the port and baud rate), Enabled or Disabled and actions. 100 per page, sortable by ID, name, station number, collection cycle and timeout.
4. Batch actions: after ticking rows, Selected N, batch enable, batch disable and batch delete appear. Only devices you may configure can be selected.
5. Form: the basic connection section holds device name (1–100 characters), area, protocol, host and port, serial parameters, S7 CPU, rack and slot, OPC UA endpoint URL, security mode, security policy, user name and password, station number and the enabled switch; advanced collection parameters are collapsed by default and hold byte order ABCD, BADC, CDAB or DCBA, collection cycle and timeout.
6. Row actions: Edit is the primary action, and Test connection sits beside it so you can check that communication works. More holds Collection diagnostics, Copy, Change collection site and Delete; OPC UA also has Browse variables. The toolbar has an OPC UA certificates entry.

■ How to use it
1. Add device: click Add device and choose an area and a protocol you may configure. Network protocols need host and port; Modbus RTU or ASCII needs serial port, baud rate, data bits, parity and stop bits; S7 needs CPU, rack and slot; OPC UA needs the endpoint URL and security settings. The save button stays grey until the name and connection address are complete.
2. Test before saving: click Test connection in the dialog and the system connects once with the current form values; a read success or connection success means the parameters are basically usable. Any form change clears the previous result and the test must be repeated.
3. After saving, the page confirms the device and offers Test read and Add tag / View tags. Run Test read first: choose the area, address and data type and confirm a raw value can be read before creating tags.
4. Entering from the collection gateways page shows only that gateway's devices and says so; Show all devices cancels the scope. Devices created this way are registered at the centre and disabled by default and must be assigned to a gateway with Change collection site; after migration they stay disabled and the address follows the target host.
5. Use disable rather than delete for a temporary stop. Deleting a single device asks to confirm deleting the device and its tags; batch delete warns that the tags below must be cleared first and lists the failures.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. Saving successfully does not mean collection works: a device is enabled but realtime monitoring shows nothing, mostly because of a wrong address, station number or byte order, or because the device is not powered. Check with Test read and Collection diagnostics instead of only raising the timeout.
2. "Port must be between 1 and 65535" or "Please fill in the host address": the host is empty or the port is out of range on a network protocol. Complete it as the manual requires and retry.
3. OPC UA connection fails: the certificate may not be trusted or the authentication mode may not match. Review and trust the server certificate on the OPC UA certificates page; user name and password authentication requires signing and encryption, so do not switch to no security mode.
4. "Please select an area you may configure": the account has no configuration permission for that area and it does not appear in the list; contact an administrator.
5. Batch actions can fail partially: a Batch results dialog lists the failures while the successful ones have taken effect; fix each item and refresh.
devices.summary: Register each PLC, instrument or gateway and tell the system how to connect to it.
devices.title: Device configuration

externalApi.body:
■ What this page is for
The external API is the channel through which other systems (MES, reporting platforms, dashboards or third-party programs) read data from this system and, when necessary, write to it. This page shows the status of REST, TCP and OPC UA and the fixed path of the OpenAPI description and manages the API keys used for access. Typical cases are connecting a new system, integration testing, giving a platform read-only access for a while and handling a leaked key. Users are usually system administrators or integration engineers: creating keys, assigning the minimum scopes and areas, adjusting the per-minute limit, disabling temporarily or revoking. Entering this page requires global system administration permission and ordinary operators do not see the menu. A key enabled state can be switched at any time; revocation cannot be undone.

■ What is on the page
1. Top: the subtitle "REST / TCP / OPC UA and API keys", with Refresh and Create API key on the right.
2. Notices: failures to load the key list, failures to load the area list and key action failures appear as red notices at the top.
3. Interface status: REST, TCP and OPC UA status, plus the OpenAPI path. REST shows Enabled or Off; TCP shows the listen address and port when enabled, otherwise Off; OPC UA shows Off, or Running or Starting with the endpoint address when enabled, marked with a green or yellow dot; OpenAPI always shows the path /openapi/v1.json.
4. Key table: name, prefix (the fixed start of the key that identifies which key appears in logs), scopes (combinations of ReadTags, ReadHistory, ReadAlarms and Write), area (All areas when empty), per-minute limit, enabled switch and actions.
5. Enabled switch: changes take effect immediately; the switch of a revoked key cannot be operated.
6. Actions column: Revoke while the key is not revoked, with the confirmation "Revocation is permanent. Continue?"; revoked keys show grey "Revoked".
7. Create API key dialog: name, scopes (four checkboxes, ReadTags reads tags, ReadHistory reads history, ReadAlarms reads alarms and Write writes), areas (multi-select, empty means all areas), per-minute limit (1–100000, default 120) and notes; Cancel and Create at the bottom.
8. Plain key dialog: titled "Copy the secret now", with the hint "The plaintext is shown once and cannot be retrieved later.", a read-only field and a Copy secret button; the Done button at the bottom closes it.

■ How to use it
1. Check the interface status first and confirm that the interface the external system needs is enabled, for example REST must show Enabled when only REST is used. This page has no start/stop switch; interfaces are configured on the server, so contact operations when the status is wrong.
2. Click Create API key, enter a name and tick the minimum scopes: read-only realtime data needs ReadTags only, historical trends also need ReadHistory, alarms also need ReadAlarms, and Write is ticked only when the other side really must write values.
3. An empty area means all areas; to limit the key to some areas select them, and removing all selected areas restores all areas.
4. Set the per-minute limit and click Create. The plain key dialog opens immediately; click Copy secret and paste it into the other system configuration, confirm "Secret copied" and click Done. After closing, the list keeps only the name and prefix and the key itself can no longer be viewed.
5. To disable temporarily, turn off the enabled switch of that row; once the external system has moved to a new key, click Revoke and confirm, and the state becomes Revoked.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. Submitting says "Enter a name and select at least one scope": the name must not be empty and at least one scope must be ticked; complete them and click Create again.
2. Copy fails with "Copy failed; select the secret text manually": the browser does not allow clipboard access; select the text in the read-only field manually. Do not close the dialog, because the plaintext cannot be obtained afterwards.
3. Before revoking, confirm that the external system has switched to a new key, because revocation is permanent. If the key is only not needed for a while, turn off the enabled switch instead of revoking.
4. Excessive permissions create risk: Write can change device setpoints, so grant it only to systems that really must write, and limit the impact with areas and the per-minute limit.
5. When "Area list could not be loaded" appears the area dropdown is incomplete; you can leave it empty for all areas and refresh and review later, so permissions are not misconfigured while not all areas are visible.
externalApi.summary: Manage the interfaces and keys external systems use, including what they can access and how fast.
externalApi.title: External API

gateways.body:
■ What this page is for
A collection gateway is a collection program deployed near the equipment. It connects to PLCs and instruments directly, packages the data and uploads it through the centre address, which suits sites where devices are far from the server, the network is unstable or the centre cannot connect directly. This page registers gateways, generates one-time keys, shows whether they are connected to the centre, whether the configuration has been applied and how much data is waiting to be transferred, and assigns devices to a gateway. The collection site in device configuration shows Gateway #id because of this assignment. This page requires global configuration permission.

■ What is on the page
1. Toolbar: search by name or ID, last refresh time and how long ago, a refresh-every-5-seconds switch, Refresh and New gateway. Above 10 seconds without a refresh the page says the status has not been updated.
2. List: gateway ID and name, process version, centre connection (Connected, not connected, disabled, pending refresh), current configuration (current configuration confirmed, not yet confirmed, pending configuration, version matches but connection lost), device count and enabled count, last heartbeat, upload backlog / centre pending (batches and bytes, not reported until the process reports).
3. Actions: Details, Edit, and the actions menu with disable or enable gateway, rotate key and release session. Release session is separated and marked in red.
4. Create and edit dialog: only the gateway name, 1–100 characters. After creating, a dialog shows the gateway ID, centre address and key to save; the key can be copied, the key record downloaded, or the dialog closed and cleared.
5. Details dialog: centre connection, last heartbeat, lease expiry, process version, configuration confirmation, remote engineering support, upload backlog, oldest pending, centre pending and configuration summary; the assigned devices below can be filtered and show protocol, tag count, state and collection hint, with Change collection site and Open device config.

■ How to use it
1. New gateway: click New gateway, enter a name and click create to generate the key. The dialog says the key is shown only once; copy it or download the key record, give the key and centre address to the field installer, then close.
2. Field connection: enter the centre address and key in the gateway program and start it. When the list shows Connected and the last heartbeat keeps updating, the lease is valid; if it shows not connected, check the address, the network and the key first.
3. Configuration: current configuration confirmed means the gateway confirmed the latest configuration; pending configuration means the digests on both sides differ, so click Refresh and look again; not yet confirmed means no configuration has ever been confirmed.
4. Assigning devices: click Change collection site in the details, or Open device config to jump to a list limited to this gateway. Migrated devices stay disabled; verify the address before enabling.
5. Replacing or reinstalling: disable the old gateway first, then consider releasing the session; before releasing you must tick that the old gateway process and field I/O have stopped. To get a new key use Rotate key, and the old key stops working immediately.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. A lost key cannot be recovered: it is shown only once when created or rotated. If the field has no record, rotate it and give the new key to the field.
2. The Release session button is grey: the confirmation that the old gateway process and field I/O have stopped is not ticked. The centre cannot confirm a field shutdown for you, so confirm it first.
3. The list keeps showing pending refresh or not connected: the network may be down, the heartbeat may have expired or the page may not have refreshed for a long time. Refresh first; if it still fails, look at the gateway report and centre handling errors, then troubleshoot devices from the collection hints in the details.
4. The field keeps transmitting after disabling: disabling only rejects the old identity at the centre, and an offline process learns about it only after reconnecting; stop the process in the field to cut it off immediately.
5. Devices in the details show pending refresh or offline / waiting: the state depends on the latest refresh or the device is not online; refresh the details and use Test read on the devices page to judge.
gateways.summary: When devices are remote or hard to reach, a gateway collects data nearby and forwards it to the centre.
gateways.title: Collection gateways

hmiLibrary.body:
■ What this page is for
Symbols & templates is the parts library for process screens. Widgets such as pumps, valves, meters and charts, and reusable panel templates, are managed and previewed here. A template is a set of arranged panel elements with placeholders (tag slots); a screen stores only which template is used and which tag each placeholder binds to. The library is saved with the project package and configuration snapshots, and publishing a screen freezes the templates and symbols used at that moment. Users are administrators with global configuration permission; the symbol and template lists on the left of the designer also come from here.

■ What is on the page
1. Top buttons: Import SVG symbol selects several .svg files at once; Import library reads a JSON library file; Export library downloads the current user library as scada-hmi-library.json and is disabled while the library is empty.
2. Built-in symbols tab: built-in ISA-101 style symbols, mainly greyscale with state colours for running and alarms; the preview state switch below offers Stopped, Running, Alarm and Unknown to check the colours of the same symbols in each state, and each symbol shows its key.
3. User library (N) tab: a table with preview, key, name, category, placeholders, modified (r version and person), referenced and actions; symbols show a thumbnail and templates show a Template tag; templates have Edit and every custom item has Delete.
4. Edit template dialog: shows the template name and placeholder tags; enter a New placeholder and click Add, and click the close on a tag to remove it; the screen designer is embedded below, where widget tag bindings are changed to placeholders; Cancel and Save template at the bottom.
5. Errors: import failures, library load failures, save failures, invalid SVG, placeholders that must be unique keys starting with a letter and placeholders still in use appear as red notices or inside the dialog.

■ How to use it
1. Browse the Built-in symbols tab first and check whether a usable widget already exists; switch the preview state to see whether the state colours match field conventions.
2. To add a symbol, click Import SVG symbol and choose the files; the system cleans the SVG (removing disallowed content), generates the key from the file name, sets the category to Custom and computes the size from the viewBox, limited to 16–400.
3. When there are several libraries or a migration from another system is under way, click Import library and choose the JSON; if the file contains keys that already exist, an overwrite confirmation appears first.
4. To reuse a set of widgets, select them in the screen designer and click Save as template; back on this page find it under User library and click Edit.
5. When editing a template, add or remove placeholders first (each must start with a letter, be unique and at most 64 characters), then bind widgets, alarms and commands to the matching placeholders in the designer, and finally click Save template.
6. To back up or migrate, click Export library and keep the downloaded JSON; restore it in the target environment with Import library.
7. Look at the Referenced column before deleting anything and confirm it is unused.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. "Placeholders must be unique keys starting with a letter": the new placeholder does not follow the naming rule (it must start with a letter, may then contain letters, digits, underscores and hyphens, and is at most 64 characters) or duplicates an existing one; rename it or delete the duplicate and retry.
2. "Placeholder X is still used by widgets, alarms, commands or other tag configuration": the placeholder still has bindings and cannot be deleted; unbind it or replace it in the designer first.
3. Deleting asks "Delete X? It is refused while screens reference it.": the server still checks references after confirmation; deletion is refused while a screen or template uses it, so remove the references first. Deleting a symbol in use may break screen display.
4. "X: invalid SVG" or "invalid file": the SVG contains disallowed content, or the JSON is neither an array nor an object with an items array; fix the file and import again, because items already imported are not rolled back automatically.
5. After saving a template, "The following screens must be republished to update the runtime version": template changes apply in the designer, but published screens use the new template only after republishing; to change a single screen, copy the template or edit the instance directly.
hmiLibrary.summary: Manage the symbols, icons and panel templates available in process screens.
hmiLibrary.title: Symbols & templates

layouts.body:
■ What this page is for
This page arranges runtime layouts: how a monitor is divided into regions, which screen or alarm list goes in each region, and how multiple monitors are arranged. Operators can use a layout in the runtime workbench only after it is published; workstation registration and assignment decide which layout opens by default. Only published screens can be bound here. Users need global configure permission.

■ What is on the page
1. Page top: explanatory text; after a successful save, "Draft saved, runtime not updated" and "Preview and publish" appear; when loading fails, an error and "Reload" are shown.
2. This PC workstation summary: name, assigned layout and version, an "Allow control / Monitor only" label, status hints (not registered, not assigned), and "Open runtime on this PC", "Edit assignment" and "Configure this workstation".
3. Unsaved local edits: N edits are staged in this browser; you can "Recover edits" or "Delete local copy". The server version is checked before recovery.
4. Layout list: search by name or runtime name and filter by publication status and workstation usage; each row shows a thumbnail, draft structure, publication status, number of workstations using it, and "Open", "Edit", "Publish" and "More". "Open" is unavailable for unpublished layouts.
5. New layout: use "Quick create workbench" (choose a screen, a name and a display mode; complete and publish in three steps), or use "New layout" to enter advanced editing.
6. Advanced editor dialog: layout name, undo/redo and runtime preview; applying a preset template replaces all monitors and regions. On the monitor tab you can set the name, grid rows and columns (1–24), add regions (up to 16 per monitor) and delete monitors; the alarm banner is fixed at the top. Region properties allow changing the ID, type (screen, alarm list, screen directory), screen, title, position and spans, and regions can be copied or deleted. At the bottom are Cancel, Save draft and Save and review for publication; issues can be clicked to locate them.
7. Workstation panel: register a workstation with a name (1–60 letters, digits, dots, underscores or hyphens), a description (up to 200 characters), an assigned published layout and allow control; list rows can be set as this PC, edited or deleted.

■ How to use it
1. Confirm that published process screens exist first; otherwise no screen can be selected for a screen region.
2. Quick creation: click "Quick create workbench", choose a screen and display mode, enter a name, preview, then "Save and review for publication" and enter a note and confirm publication as prompted.
3. Advanced editing: click "New layout", expand advanced parameters, set the monitor count, grid and regions, choose published screens for screen regions, adjust position and size, then click "Save draft".
4. Handle issues: when the page reports "N issues must be handled before publication", clicking an item switches to the monitor, expands the parameters and locates the field automatically; fix it and save again.
5. Publishing: click "Publish" on a list row, check screen references and workstation impact, enter a note of 1–500 characters, and confirm to create a new published version.
6. Assign workstations: register or edit one in the "Workstation" panel, select a published layout and click "Set as this PC"; once the summary shows that runtime uses the published version, click "Open runtime on this PC".
7. Verify: the list row shows "Published VX"; click "Open" to enter the runtime workbench. After changing a layout, publish again for the change to take effect.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. "Save draft" is not publishing: the list still shows unpublished or draft changes and a workstation cannot open the runtime page; you must click "Publish" and complete the review and note.
2. Publication is blocked: common causes are a region outside the grid or overlapping, an empty or duplicate ID, a grid outside 1–24, more than 16 regions, or a screen that is not a published screen. A draft can be staged, but it cannot be published until these are fixed.
3. When changing the grid, "The grid will change from A×B to C×D and the following regions will be out of bounds" appears: "Keep region positions" keeps the out-of-bounds content, "Fit regions to the grid" scales it into the grid, and "Cancel" keeps the original grid.
4. If "Server draft updated" appears or a delete returns a conflict: click "Reload draft" or "Reload lists", check the content and retry; the system does not merge automatically.
5. Local edits are stored per account in this browser; unsaved edits may be lost on refresh or on another PC. When the server version changes, the page offers to recover them as a new independent draft. If a workstation has control disabled, its control requests are rejected and audited by the server.
layouts.summary: Arrange screens and alarm strips into a workbench so operators can see a whole line at a glance.
layouts.title: Workbench configuration

license.body:
■ What this page is for
The software license page confirms whether this SCADA system has a valid license, how long it remains valid, and how many devices and tags may connect. The server determines the state; this page only displays it and provides the activation entry point. Administrators use it to check the remaining allowance before delivery, renewal or expansion, and field operators come here to copy the machine ID and request a new activation code from the vendor when the "License invalid" message appears. While the license is invalid, all features except the sign-in page and this page stop, so this page is the only way to restore operation. The device limit and tag limit here are the totals that device configuration and tag configuration may register.

■ What is on the page
1. Status label: to the right of the title it shows Licensed, Expiring soon, Trial, Expired, Invalid or Clock anomaly. Clock anomaly usually means the server clock was adjusted or the certificate time does not match.
2. Notice bar: the license message returned by the server, red when invalid, yellow when expiring soon, green otherwise.
3. License information: machine ID, license ID, customer, expiry, days remaining, device limit and tag limit. "Copy" sits to the right of the machine ID; a limit that is empty or 0 shows "Unlimited".
4. Licensed features: lists the licensed features separated by slashes; with no add-on features it shows "Base features".
5. Trial expiry: shown only when the status is Trial, with the trial end time.
6. Enter activation code: visible only to administrators with user-management permission, a four-line text box plus an "Activate" button; other accounts see only the blue hint "Only an administrator with user-management permission can activate the software."
7. Reminder dialog: after sign-in, if the license is expiring soon or 15 or fewer trial days remain, "License expiring soon" appears with the machine ID, expiry and days remaining, and offers "Don't remind me today" or "Activate"; when the license is invalid, a non-closable "License invalid" dialog appears and only "Activate" is offered.

■ How to use it
1. Read the status label first: green Licensed is normal; yellow Expiring soon needs renewal soon; red Expired, Invalid or Clock anomaly needs reactivation.
2. To request a license, click "Copy" next to the machine ID and send the machine ID, site name, expected device count and tag count to the vendor. Success shows "Machine ID copied"; failure shows "Copy failed. Select the text manually." In that case select the text with the mouse and copy it yourself.
3. When the activation code arrives, paste it into the box (it starts with SCADA1.) and click "Activate". The button is disabled when the box is empty or contains only spaces, and shows a loading state while submitting.
4. Successful activation refreshes the information in place, shows "Activated" and clears the local "Don't remind me today" record. Then check the four items: expiry, days remaining, device and tag limits, and licensed features, and return to device configuration and tag configuration to confirm the current counts are within the limits.
5. If "Activation failed. Check the activation code and try again." appears, first confirm the code is complete, has no extra spaces or line breaks, and was issued for the current machine ID; if it still fails, ask the vendor to reissue it.
6. If "Could not load license information" appears when opening the page, the interface returned no data; refresh the page or contact operations to check the service. This is a read error and does not mean the license is invalid.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. Only administrators with user-management permission can activate. Operators and viewers can only read the information; ask an administrator to sign in, or grant user-management permission to the relevant role under Areas and roles.
2. While the license is invalid, all features except sign-in and this page stop. Do not keep refreshing other pages; activate on this page directly. Features resume automatically after success, with no service restart.
3. The machine ID is bound to the server. Replacing the server, reinstalling the system or changing server hardware changes the machine ID, and the old activation code usually no longer works; provide the new machine ID and request a new code.
4. When "Clock anomaly" rather than "Expired" is shown, check the server and operating-system time and time zone first; an incorrect clock also triggers this state. Fix it and refresh to confirm.
5. An activation code is a credential; do not share it or use one code on several machines. When reporting a problem, provide the license ID and customer name so the vendor can check.
license.summary: Check licence state, machine code, expiry and device/tag limits, and enter an activation code.
license.title: Software license

measurementReports.body:
■ What this page is for
Tag statistics is an ad hoc query page that answers questions such as "what were the average, minimum and maximum of this temperature yesterday". It aggregates the history of selected tags into a table by day or by month and can export to Excel, which suits inspection rounds, shift handover and quick checks; it is not formal archiving. For formal business reports, scheduled generation, archiving and sign-off, use Business reports; buttons at the top right of both pages link to each other. Users are usually shift staff, process engineers and managers who need ad hoc data. The page requires no extra configure permission, only sign-in and visibility of tags; the tags available are set by the account's data access permissions.

■ What is on the page
1. Top: the "Tag statistics" title and a "Business reports" button on the right; below, text explains that daily/monthly tag statistics can be queried and exported to Excel, and that fixed business templates and formal archives belong in Business reports.
2. Report type: the radio options "Daily report" and "Monthly report". Switching type resets the time range to that type's default.
3. Time range: a date range for daily reports and a month range for monthly reports; shortcuts are "Today", "Yesterday" and "Last 7 days" for daily, and "This month", "Last month" and "Last 3 months" for monthly.
4. Tag selection: searchable, multi-select and clearable, with selected items collapsed; options show as "#ID · device / tag" and calculation tags with no device show "Calculation tag". The first 3 tags are selected by default after loading.
5. Status line: "Loading devices and tags…" while loading, otherwise "x / y tags selected" or a validation hint such as "Select at least one tag", "Select a time range" or "Select a valid time range; the end time cannot be earlier than the start time".
6. Buttons: "Reload tags" appears when loading fails; the primary button is "Generate report"; "Export Excel" is disabled when there is no result, conditions changed, loading/exporting, or the query failed.
7. Result: shows the report type, range, "n aggregated rows" and "Last generated: time · m tags"; the table columns are time (sortable), tag, average, minimum, maximum and sample count, with values to 3 decimal places. The empty state reports no available tags, no query yet, no data, or a load/query failure.

■ How to use it
1. Choose daily or monthly first. Switching type resets the time range to the default; select another range manually if needed.
2. Choose the time range: daily reports count whole days at both ends (including the whole end date), monthly reports count whole months; shortcuts give common ranges.
3. Search and tick tags in the dropdown; the status line shows the selected count. The first 3 tags are selected on first open, and you can clear and reselect.
4. Click "Generate report"; when it finishes the table shows data together with "n aggregated rows" and the last successful generation time.
5. Check that time, tag, average, minimum, maximum and sample count are reasonable; a small sample count has limited statistical value.
