6. Click "Export Excel" when the data must go to someone else. Export uses the conditions of the last successful generation, and the file name includes the report type and start/end dates; if conditions were just changed, generate again before exporting.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. The button stays grey and the page says "Select at least one tag" or "Select a time range": the conditions are incomplete and "Generate report" will not run. Select tags and a range to enable the button.
2. The table did not change after changing tags or time and "Filter conditions changed" appears: the page keeps the last generated result and the export button is disabled accordingly. The hint disappears after clicking "Generate report" again.
3. "No tags available; check tag configuration or access permission": the account cannot see tags or the list is empty. Click "Reload tags" first; if it stays empty, ask an administrator to check tag configuration and area authorization.
4. After a failed query the table may still hold the previous data, and an empty table shows "Report query failed" or "Export failed". Follow the red hint, and if needed narrow the time range and tag count before retrying.
5. A daily report includes the whole end date and a monthly report the whole end month; if you think only the previous day or the current day was queried, check the range line and the data times in the result. Long ranges and many tags are slower, so verify with a few tags before expanding.
measurementReports.summary: Temporarily query the average, minimum and maximum of tags over a period and export to Excel.
measurementReports.title: Tag statistics

notifications.body:
■ What this page is for
Alarm notifications deliver alarms beyond the screen: besides the on-screen warning, email, SMS or webhook can reach people who are not at a computer. The page has four parts: routes decide which channel is used for which level, area, shift and recipients; channels define the mail server or HTTP address; shifts limit when messages are sent; delivery failures list notifications whose retries are exhausted. It works together with "Alarm rules" and "Annunciators": rules decide what is an alarm, and this page handles delivery. Users are usually system administrators or area owners. Channels and shifts are global configuration, and area configurers can manage only routes in areas they are allowed.

■ What is on the page
1. Four tabs: Notification routes, Notification channels, Shifts and Delivery failures; the last tab title carries the count of unhandled records.
2. The Notification routes tab explains that routes send by level, area and shift, and a route with an escalation time sends once only when an alarm stays unacknowledged that long. "Add route" on the right is disabled when there is no channel or no configure permission, and hints that a channel must be created first.
3. Route table: name, area, minimum level, shift, channel, trigger, recipients, enabled and actions. An empty area shows "All areas" and an empty shift shows "Any"; a trigger with an escalation time shows "Escalate after N min unacknowledged", otherwise "Alarm / recovery".
4. Route dialog: name, channel (required), area (empty means all areas and needs global permission), minimum level (Info, Warning, Critical), shift (empty means any), recipients, escalation switch and minutes, send timing and enabled. Recipients are hidden when the channel is Webhook.
5. The Notification channels tab notes that credentials are stored encrypted and the page shows only ***. "New channel" is available only with global configure permission. The table columns are name, type, address, credentials, enabled and actions; actions are edit, test and delete.
6. Channel dialog: name, type (Email (SMTP), Webhook, SMS), timeout (ms) and enabled. Email needs the SMTP server, port, SSL/STARTTLS, sender, account and password; other types need the URL, auth header name and value. When credentials already exist, "Clear saved credentials" can be ticked.
7. The Shifts tab allows adding only with global configure permission; the table columns are name, time, weekday, enabled and actions. The dialog takes name, start and end time (half-hour steps), weekdays and enabled, and notes at the bottom that an end earlier than the start means crossing midnight, with the weekday taken from the start day.
8. The Delivery failures tab explains notifications whose retries are exhausted: failures not acknowledged within the last 24 hours raise a health-check alarm, and acknowledging them stops the alarm. It offers "Refresh" and "Acknowledge all"; columns are alarm, action, count, last error, failure time and actions.

■ How to use it
1. Create a channel first: click "New channel", choose the type and enter the address. After saving, click "Test" to verify connectivity.
2. Then create a route: click "Add route", enter a name, choose a channel, optionally an area and shift, and set the minimum level and recipients (separated by commas or line breaks).
3. Decide the timing: to notify the next level when an alarm stays unacknowledged, turn on "Escalate when unacknowledged" and enter minutes (1–10080); otherwise tick one or both of alarm and recovery.
4. When messages should be sent only within certain times, create a shift on the Shifts tab first, then select it in the route.
5. Verify: saving a route shows "Saved" and the new row appears in the list; then use the channel test to confirm recipients receive the message.
6. Handle failures: read the last error and count, fix the channel or network, then click "Acknowledge" or "Acknowledge all"; the page shows "N records acknowledged".

■ Good to know and common issues
1. "Add route" is grey: there may be no channel yet, or the account has neither global configure permission nor a configurable area. Create a channel on Notification channels first.
2. Credentials show only ***: the page never displays them. When editing other fields, leave the field empty to keep the current value; to clear it, tick "Clear saved credentials". On creation, empty means no credentials.
3. The test asks for a recipient: email and SMS tests require one, Webhook does not. A test sends a real message, so do not disturb unrelated people.
4. Save or delete fails: usually a required field is empty or the area is not permitted; the exact error appears at the top of the dialog and the page.
5. Delivery failures show the last error: retries have reached the limit. Use the channel test to identify the problem, then acknowledge the record after handling it.
notifications.summary: Send alarms by email, SMS or webhook and decide who receives them and when.
notifications.title: Alarm notifications

objectTemplateEditor.body:
■ What this page is for
The object template editor defines the makeup of a typical device: which tags it has and their relative offsets and data types, which alarms it carries, and which widgets its faceplate uses. Templates store no absolute addresses; the instance supplies the base address, so the real address is "instance base + relative offset", which lets devices of the same type share configuration and be revised together. The page manages drafts and publications: changes are saved as a draft first, publishing creates a read-only version snapshot, and existing objects follow through previewed upgrades. Entering this page requires global configure permission; addresses, types and archiving directly affect collection and history storage.

■ What is on the page
1. Top: "Templates" returns to the list on the left; the template name box accepts up to 100 characters; an "Unsaved" or "Saved" state label; "Draft rN · latest vN or None"; on the right "Validate template", "Save template" and "Publish new version".
2. A hint bar explains that logical keys are used for matching across versions and the base address is supplied by the instance.
3. Four tabs: Tag definitions, Alarm definitions, Faceplate template and Publication history.
4. Tag definition table columns: logical key, name, area, offset, OPC NodeId, type, S7 DB, S7 bit, unit, multiplier, offset value, low limit, high limit, writable, archive, archive deadband, archive seconds, description and actions. Areas include Coil, Discrete input, Holding register, Input register, S7 DB, S7 M, S7 I, S7 Q and OPC UA node; types include Boolean, Int16, UInt16, Int32, UInt32, Float and Double. The DB number shows only for S7 DB; the S7 bit (0–7) shows only for Boolean tags in S7 areas; NodeId shows only for OPC UA nodes and supports {instance} and {address}. Booleans hide unit, multiplier, offset and limits. Archiving can be No storage, Store on change or Periodic storage, and only periodic storage takes archive seconds. The writable switch is forced off for read-only areas such as discrete input, input register and S7 I, and changing the type clears the S7 bit.
5. Alarm definition table columns: logical key, tag, type, threshold, level, delay (s), return deadband, message, enabled and actions. The tag can only be a logical key of this template; types are High-high limit, High limit, Low limit, Low-low limit and State change, and State change hides the threshold; levels are Info, Warning and Critical.
6. The Faceplate template tab embeds the screen designer, where template tags can be used as widget binding sources; widgets are copied with the template into every object's faceplate.
7. Publication history lists published version, time, publisher and "View version"; snapshots are read-only and show the tag and alarm counts.

■ How to use it
1. Click "Add template tag" and fill in the logical key (avoid changing it after publication), name, area, offset and type. For booleans watch the bit offset; for analog values watch multiplier, offset and limits.
2. Click "Add template alarm" and choose the tag, type, threshold (except state change), level, delay, return deadband, message and enabled.
3. When a faceplate is needed, switch to Faceplate template, lay it out in the designer and bind template tags.
4. Click "Validate template"; the dialog lists issues, showing "Validation passed" when all pass. Fix as prompted and validate again.
5. Click "Save template"; the page shows "Template draft saved". Structural errors are also listed in the validation dialog.
6. Click "Publish new version". Unsaved changes are saved automatically first, and publication stops if that save fails; success shows "Template vN published".
7. Verify: return to the template list and confirm the version marker shows "Published vN", then run a previewed upgrade on the object instances page.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. "The template has unsaved changes. Leave anyway?" on exit: the draft differs from the saved content. Choose "Continue editing" to keep it, or "Leave" to discard it.
2. Publication produced no new version: usually the automatic save was rejected or validation failed; check the items in the template validation, fix them and publish again.
3. The writable switch cannot be changed: read-only areas such as discrete input, input register and S7 I are forced off when loaded; use a holding register or S7 Q instead.
4. The alarm tag dropdown is empty: the template has no tags yet; add and save tags before binding.
5. Addresses do not match the field: templates store relative offsets, and the absolute address is the instance base plus the offset; check the base address on the Device objects & templates page.
objectTemplateEditor.summary: Edit tags, alarms and panels in a device template, then validate, save and publish a new version.
objectTemplateEditor.title: Object template editor

objectTemplates.body:
■ What this page is for
Device objects & templates handles "many identical devices". Ten pumps of the same model may share the same tag list, alarm rules and faceplate structure and differ only in the starting address; create one template and generate in bulk instead of configuring each device by hand. Templates store only relative offsets; when objects are generated, the real address is the collection device's base address plus the offset, and later revisions only need a template change and an upgrade. The page manages templates and versions on one side and generated objects and upgrades on the other. It suits engineers and instrument technicians who create tags in a batch during commissioning. Bulk-generated faceplates are drafts only and must be checked and published in the screen designer before they appear in the runtime.

■ What is on the page
1. Top: "Refresh" and "New template". Creation takes a template name, default example "Pump template", 1–100 characters; on success it opens the editor.
2. Device templates tab: cards show the template name, version, object instance count and update time. The version shows "Published vN" or "Draft". Card actions are edit template, bulk generate objects (disabled without a published version) and delete.
3. Object instances tab: filter by "All templates"; "Upgrade selected" requires ticking objects first. Columns are object name, collection device, source template, base address, version and actions. The version shows "Applied vA / latest vB" and turns yellow when behind.
4. Instance row actions: "Faceplate draft" opens the screen designer; "Preview upgrade" is disabled when already on the latest version; "Unlink" keeps tags, alarms and faceplates after confirmation and only stops following template upgrades.
5. Bulk generation dialog: template version, collection device, name prefix, start number, object count, start base address and address spacing, with a live list of object names, base addresses and tag address ranges. Object names are the prefix plus a number of at least two digits.
6. The preview result shows "x tags / y alarms / z widgets" and "Can generate" or "Needs correction" for each object, listing the reasons when generation is not possible.
7. Template upgrade preview dialog: shows the selected count and target version, and per object "Upgradable" or "Items pending", errors and a change list; conflicts show a three-way comparison of the generation baseline, the current field configuration and the new template, with the choices "Keep field (unlink on removal)" or "Adopt template (delete config on removal)".

■ How to use it
1. Click "New template", enter a name, open the editor, add tags, alarms and a faceplate, then publish a new version.
2. Back on this page click "Bulk generate objects", choose the template version and collection device, and set the prefix, start number, count, start base address and address spacing (the base difference between adjacent objects).
3. Click "Preview generation" and confirm that the address range does not exceed 65535 and every object can be generated, then click "Confirm generation". Success shows "Generated N objects; device faceplates await review and publish" and switches to the object instances tab.
4. Verify: check the object count, base addresses and version, open "Faceplate draft" to check bindings, and publish in the screen designer after confirming.
5. Upgrade: tick objects of the same template, click "Upgrade selected", choose the target version, click "Preview upgrade", resolve conflicts and click "Preview again", then click "Confirm upgrade" once all are upgradable.
6. When an object really must leave the template, click "Unlink" and confirm.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. A yellow hint in the preview usually means no collection device was selected, the count is outside 1–100, base address plus the template's largest offset exceeds 65535, an object name exceeds 40 characters, or a name has leading or trailing spaces. The hint disappears and the button enables after fixing.
2. "Confirm generation" is grey: a successful preview is required first; changing parameters invalidates the old preview, so preview again.
3. "Select objects of the same template each time": an upgrade accepts instances of one template only; select them separately or filter by template first.
4. "The selected objects already use the latest version, or have no common higher version": the objects are already current, or the versions differ too much to share an upgradable version.
5. Deleting a template fails: linked instances still exist; unlink them or clean up the objects first.
objectTemplates.summary: Use template plus batch generation to create tags, alarms and panels for many similar devices at once.
objectTemplates.title: Device objects & templates

oee.body:
■ What this page is for
OEE production serves production managers, shift leaders and process staff. OEE is Overall Equipment Effectiveness, the product of Availability A (the share of planned time the equipment actually ran), Performance P (the run speed relative to the ideal cycle) and Quality Q (the share of good product). Low A usually means downtime, low P usually means speed loss or idling, and low Q usually means scrap. The page summarizes by line, product, shift and time range with trends, a downtime Pareto and grouped detail, which suits post-shift review and exception investigation. Base data comes from OEE configuration, and daily downtime and output corrections are entered under Production events; use this page to locate the gap, then handle the detail on the events page.

■ What is on the page
1. Top: "Production events", "Excel" and "PDF". "Production events" appears only with control permission and carries the current or last queried time range and line; export buttons are disabled before a query, after conditions change, or while loading/exporting.
2. Filter bar: time range, "24 hours / 7 days / 30 days" shortcuts, area, line, product and shift dropdowns (lines follow the area) and "Query".
3. Hints: when conditions changed without querying, "Filter conditions changed; the previous result is still shown, query again before exporting" appears; after a query, "Result range: … Area: … Line: …"; when rollups are used, "Earlier parts of long ranges use rollups; detail starts at the recent window".
4. Core cards: OEE, Availability, Performance and Quality with percentage, target xx% and "On target / Below target / No data"; an asterisk on Performance means it was capped at 100%. Supporting metrics are good count, scrap rate, run/planned (h), MTBF/MTTR (mean time between failures and mean time to repair), failure count and production vs target (%).
5. Charts are the OEE trend (OEE, A, P and Q lines) and the downtime Pareto (downtime hours as bars with a cumulative share line); "No data for this range" covers the chart when there is no planned time or output.
6. Tabs: Downtime reasons shows code, name, category, hours, count, share and cumulative share; By shift, By product and By day show OEE and good count, and each day row has "View day", which switches to that day and queries automatically, with "Back to previous range" to return.

■ How to use it
1. Choose the line and time range; use "24 hours / 7 days" for daily review and "30 days" for monthly analysis, then click "Query". Continue once the result range and metric cards appear.
2. Compare OEE with A, P and Q: investigate the metric below target in the direction of downtime, speed or quality, and use run/planned hours, failure count and scrap rate as evidence.
3. Read the downtime Pareto and the Downtime reasons tab to find the largest and fastest-growing reasons; compare with By shift, By product and By day, and click "View day" for an abnormal day, then "Back to previous range".
4. To add missing downtime or correct output, click "Production events", then return and click "Query" again to confirm the change; use "Excel" or "PDF" to keep a record, which downloads the last queried result.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. All metrics show "—" with "No planned production time or output recorded for this range; OEE cannot be calculated": check that the line shifts are enabled in OEE configuration, that they cover the range, and that output counter tags are bound, then query again.
2. The result did not change after changing conditions: the page shows only the last queried result and export is disabled. Click "Query" again; export is enabled once the yellow hint disappears.
3. An asterisk after Performance means the value exceeded 100% and was capped; adjust "Performance capped at 100%" under OEE thresholds in OEE configuration. Turning it off may produce performance above 100%.
4. Early detail is missing for long ranges: the early part is rolled up and detail starts at the recent window. Shorten the range to check details, or drill into a specific day with By day.
5. A query reports "Select a valid time range; the end time must be later than the start time": select a correct range. If export fails, the reason returned by the server appears at the top of the page.
oee.summary: Use OEE to measure how much of the planned time ran, how fast it ran, and how much good product came out.
oee.title: OEE production

oeeConfig.body:
■ What this page is for
OEE configuration maintains the base dictionary for OEE statistics, for engineers or production administrators with area configure permission. The system must know the lines, the products made, how shifts are divided, how downtime reasons are classified and what targets to meet before it can calculate OEE. This page maintains only these base items; daily downtime entry, reason classification and output corrections belong to Production events, and the two must not be mixed. Configuration changes affect later statistics, so delete carefully. Entry requires configure permission for at least one area; without it the page cannot be opened and table buttons are hidden per row.

■ What is on the page
1. Top: the "OEE configuration" title, a "Production events" button on the right (shown with control permission) and an "OEE thresholds" button (shown only with global configure permission).
2. Lines tab: the table shows name, area, ideal cycle (s), enabled (Yes/No) and actions. "Add" opens a dialog for the name, area, ideal cycle (s), optional products and the enabled switch.
3. Products tab: the table shows name, code and ideal cycle (s). The dialog takes name, code, area (global permission may leave it empty for "Global (all areas)") and ideal cycle (s).
4. Shifts tab: the table shows name, area and time window (start and end minutes formatted as HH:MM). The dialog takes name, area, start minute, end minute (0–1439) and the enabled switch.
5. Downtime reasons tab: the table shows code, name, category (Availability / Performance / Quality) and planned downtime (Yes/No). The dialog takes code, name, category, area (empty with global permission) and the "Planned downtime" switch.
6. OEE thresholds dialog: target OEE, target availability, target performance and target quality as four decimals between 0 and 1 (adjusted by 0.01) and the "Performance capped at 100%" switch; saving carries the version number so concurrent edits do not overwrite each other.

■ How to use it
1. Create lines first: on the Lines tab click "Add", choose the area, enter the name and ideal cycle (s), confirm that "Enabled" is on and save. The ideal cycle is the shortest time in which one device should make one product and is the basis for Performance; the row appears after a successful save.
2. Then create products: add on the Products tab with name, code and ideal cycle; leaving the area empty means all areas (global configure permission only).
3. Configure shifts: add on the Shifts tab; the area is required and start and end are entered as minutes of the day (for example 480 for 08:00 and 1200 for 20:00); after saving the time window column shows the corresponding times.
4. Configure downtime reasons: add on the Downtime reasons tab; code and name are required, and the category decides whether the reason counts toward availability, performance or quality. Planned downtime means scheduled downtime and is not counted as unplanned loss. After saving it can be selected under Production events.
5. Set targets: with global configure permission click "OEE thresholds", adjust the four targets and the cap switch and save. Queries on OEE production then show "Target xx%" and the on-target state on the cards.
6. Click "Edit" to fix an entry; click "Delete" and confirm for an entry no longer used, then check that it disappears from the list.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. Deleting reports "Delete failed": the entry is still referenced by history or other data. Turn "Enabled" off instead of deleting, so history keeps its attribution.
2. "Ideal cycle or rated output must be set": the ideal cycle of lines and products must be greater than 0 (the input minimum is 0.001), and an empty or 0 value is rejected. Enter the actual cycle and save.
3. Saving thresholds reports "Version conflict… close the dialog, reopen it and edit again": someone else changed the thresholds. Close and reopen the dialog to read the latest values, then edit and save.
4. The area dropdown offers only a few options when adding: it lists only areas the account may configure. Without global permission the area of products and reasons cannot be empty, and "Global (all areas)" cannot be selected.
5. Shifts validate only the name and area; start and end minutes must be between 0 and 1439 and "end later than start" is not enforced; fill crossing midnight according to the site convention.
oeeConfig.summary: Create lines, products, shifts, downtime reasons and OEE targets before the statistics can work.
oeeConfig.title: OEE configuration

ops.body:
■ What this page is for
This page keeps the system collecting and controlling when hardware or services fail. When two servers run as primary and standby, the primary provides collection and control while the standby continuously replicates configuration and history and can take over at any time. The page shows primary/standby state and offers manual switchover, and below are backup and recovery drills that verify whether a backup package can be restored. It is for system maintainers and requires global system maintenance permission.

■ What is on the page
1. Primary/standby state: a role label (Primary, Standby, Single node) to the right of the title, with the node ID and term beside it. The term is the round number of the primary election and increases with each switchover. "Refresh" is at the top right; only the primary shows "Switch to standby" and only the standby shows "Take over on this node".
2. Single-node hint: when primary/standby is not enabled, "Single-node deployment: primary/standby not enabled" appears and no details are shown.
3. State fields: peer (node, role, term; "Unreachable" when it cannot be read), peer address, last heartbeat, quorum (a third-party witness node; "None" when not configured), lease (holder and expiry), automatic switching, configuration replication (last sync time and applied count), history replication (rows behind) and switchover count.
4. Abnormal hints: red "Quorum unavailable" when quorum is lost; yellow "Replication failed" when replication is abnormal, usually a network or peer load problem.
5. Event list: time, type (start, stop, promote, demote, handover), content, term and operator ("System" when there is no record).
6. Backup and recovery drill: beside the title, the off-site target is described as "name (directory or object storage, keeping N copies)", or "Not configured"; "Back up and drill now" backs up immediately and runs verification.
7. Backup record table and local backup package table: the former has time, trigger, package size, recovery drill (passed with duration, failed, not drilled), off-site target label (red on failure) and notes; the latter lists files, size and "Recovery drill".
8. At the bottom, a hint states that Prometheus scrapes /metrics, which requires Scada:MetricsToken to be configured and Bearer access.

■ How to use it
1. During inspection click "Refresh" and read the role label, last heartbeat and quorum; a heartbeat that does not update for a long time means the peer is unreachable, and quorum showing "None" means only manual switching is possible. Also check the applied count of configuration replication and the rows behind in history replication.
2. To maintain the primary, click "Switch to standby"; the dialog requires a reason (up to 200 characters, written to the audit log) and notes that "This node will stop collection and control; the standby takes over after its final sync". Before confirming, verify that the standby is online and that rows behind are 0 or small; after "Confirm" the page shows "Completed", a handover or promote record appears in the event list, and the role label becomes Standby.
3. On the standby, "Take over on this node" is for an unavailable primary. If the primary is online the request is forwarded to it for a normal switchover; if it is offline, quorum must confirm that the lease has expired, and a reason is still required. With quorum configured, a failure fails directly; only without quorum does "Force takeover" appear, warning that "Confirm the original primary is stopped before forcing takeover, otherwise two primaries may exist".
4. Backup drill: click "Back up and drill now". A complete pass shows "Backup completed and passed the recovery drill"; if the backup succeeds but the drill or a target fails, red "Backup completed with problems" appears with details. Without an off-site target the backup stays on this machine.
5. Verify: the recovery drill column of the newest row should be green "Passed", and the number of off-site labels should match the configured targets and all be green.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. Prefer switching the primary before maintenance. Stopping the primary directly relies on automatic switching; when automatic switching is off the standby does not take over and collection stops until someone acts.
2. "Force takeover" may create two primaries. Use it only when quorum is unavailable and the original primary is confirmed stopped; when both serve at once, devices may be written twice and the cause is hard to find afterwards.
3. Switchover and takeover require a reason, which is written to the audit log; an empty or over-long reason (more than 200 characters) shows "Enter a reason" and the action is not submitted.
4. A backup drill is not only about whether the backup succeeded. When "Backup completed with problems" appears, do not just confirm the files exist; fix the items listed in the notes and run it again.
5. Primary/standby state refreshes automatically every 5 seconds; a failed refresh shows only "Could not load primary/standby state" and does not clear backup records. An operation reporting "Operations action failed" is usually an interface timeout or a service error.
ops.summary: Check primary/standby servers, switch over, inspect replication and run backup drills.
ops.title: Operations & HA

overview.body:
■ What this page is for
The Overview is the plant dashboard: it brings together whether devices are online, whether there are alarms and whether the system is healthy. Checking it first at shift start, handover or during inspection rounds saves the most time. It summarizes online devices, active unacknowledged alarms, recovered but unacknowledged alarms, suppressed or shelved alarms, plus channel backlog, history storage and uptime; from an abnormal card you can go to Realtime, Alarms or trend curves. Operators, engineers and administrators all use it, but whether a card navigates depends on the account's permission for the target page. The page refreshes every 5 seconds, pauses when the tab goes to the background, and catches up once when it returns.

■ What is on the page
1. Top update bar: the last complete update time, taken as the earliest successful refresh among device health, alarm lists and alarm statistics, so all three parts are up to date. "Data is stale" appears when a complete refresh has not happened for more than 15 seconds or any interface failed; the round button on the right refreshes.
2. Errors and warnings: each of the three data groups has its own hint when it fails; when statistics fail, the page says it estimates from the loaded portion, not the whole plant; system health warnings are also listed.
3. Alarm flood banner: appears when alarm flooding or area flood governance occurs, with the statistics window, triggered count, threshold, suppressed count, first-out alarm and clear condition. "View alarms and flood details" opens the Alarms page.
4. Four statistic cards: device online shows online / total, orange on the left when any device is offline and red when all are offline; active unacknowledged turns red when above 0 and opens the "Active unacknowledged" filter; recovered awaiting acknowledgement is orange on the left when non-zero and "View handling" opens it; suppressed / shelved shows two counts and the button changes to "Alarm flood" during a flood, opening the "Suppressed" filter.
5. Statistics notes: active unacknowledged excludes recovered awaiting acknowledgement, shelved and suppressed; alarm flooding is judged by recent trigger frequency and differs from the current active count.
6. Current active alarms: sorted by Critical, Warning and Info, showing at most the first 10. Each row has level, alarm message and source (device / tag or system event), trigger value, start time and state (unacknowledged or active acknowledged). When the alarm has a tag and a screen can be opened, the row's primary action is Open screen; otherwise it is Open alarm. Trend and the other action are under More.
7. Device communication state: "Only abnormal" is on by default and lists only offline devices or devices with errors. Columns are device, state, last collection, cycle, communication failures and error message; the state is Online, Offline or grey "Data is stale". Clicking the device name opens Realtime. Offline devices come first, then devices with errors, then the rest by name.
8. Maintenance metrics (collapsed): configured tag count and channel backlog, history storage used and disk free, uptime and runtime environment. Channel backlog turns orange on the left when above 0, disk free turns red below 5 GB, and the storage card opens System administration.
9. Quick entries (collapsed): cards for common pages; the star toggles a favorite and favorites appear under Favorites; the "Search" button opens page search (shortcut Ctrl+K).
10. Configuration guide: visible only to accounts with configure permission; it shows completion state for steps such as devices, tags, alarms and screens, offers "Verify" on configurable devices to see the result, and opens the matching configuration page or collection diagnostics.

■ How to use it
1. At shift handover or during inspection, read the update bar first. If "Data is stale" appears, click refresh; otherwise use the statistic cards to set priorities, handling red cards or large numbers first.
2. Handling alarms: click the "Active unacknowledged" card to open the Alarms page and acknowledge alarms one by one; you can also open that row's More and click Trend to see the curve before and after the alarm. After returning to the Overview the unacknowledged count should drop; if it does not, check for recovered awaiting acknowledgement or shelved records.
3. Handling offline devices: find the offline device under device communication state and click its name to open Realtime. Read the error message and last sample time, then troubleshoot with collection diagnostics; after fixing, click refresh and confirm the online count rises and the error disappears.
4. Handling alarm floods: acknowledge the most severe alarms first, then shelve or suppress nuisance alarms. Click "View alarms and flood details" in the banner to check the trigger count and threshold of the last 10 minutes.
5. Watch capacity: expand maintenance metrics; a channel backlog above 0 means collected data is queuing on the bus, so check server load or the network; when disk free falls below 5 GB, click the card to open System administration and check usage and retention.
6. Customize quick entries: click the star to add a favorite and click again to remove it; favorites are stored only for the current account in this browser and do not follow you to another PC.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. Overview numbers do not match the Alarms page: the Overview alarm list reads at most 200 records and the table shows only the first 10; when statistics fail the page falls back to an estimate from the loaded portion. When "Loaded portion only" or "Alarm statistics unavailable" appears, trust the results queried by state on the Alarms page.
2. "Data is stale" appears: more than 15 seconds passed without a complete refresh, an interface failed, or the tab was paused in the background. Returning to the foreground catches up automatically and you can also refresh manually; if it still fails, follow the error hint.
3. Statistic cards do not navigate: the account has no permission for the target page and the cards are display-only. Ask an administrator to grant access if navigation is needed.
4. No normal devices appear after turning on "Only abnormal": that is the default behavior; turn it off to show all. "Data is stale" means health data was not obtained this time and does not mean the device is stopped.
5. The alarm count does not fall: recovered awaiting acknowledgement or shelved / suppressed records may remain. Click "View handling" on those two cards respectively and check again after handling.
overview.summary: A dashboard for the whole plant. Start here at shift handover or during rounds to see what is healthy and what needs attention.
overview.title: Overview

productionEvents.body:
■ What this page is for
The Production events page is the production ledger for shift leaders and duty staff and keeps only downtime events. How long a device stopped, why, whether it counts as a fault or changeover, and whether already counted output must be increased or decreased are entered and confirmed here. OEE statistics read this data directly, so whether records are timely and correctly classified affects Availability and Quality. Entering from the "Production events" button on OEE production carries the current time range and line; entering from OEE configuration does not carry them and uses the default last 7 days and all lines. The page requires control permission for at least one area, and whether a row can be edited depends on control permission for that line's area.

■ What is on the page
1. Top: the "Production events" title and an "OEE production" button on the right to return to the statistics page.
2. Filter bar: line dropdown (clearable, showing all lines), time range (last 7 days by default, separator "to", placeholders "Start" and "End"), confirmation state (All confirmation states / Pending / Confirmed) and "Query".
3. Notice bar: after conditions change it shows "Filter conditions changed; click Query; the table still shows the previous result"; at 2000 records it shows "The 2000-record display limit is reached; narrow the time range or filter by line and query again"; query or load failures show a red error above the table.
4. Action buttons: "Add" and "Output correction" appear when there is a controllable line.
5. Downtime event table: line, start/end time (an unfinished event shows "Event still running" on the second line), duration (minutes, growing in real time while unfinished), reason ("Unclassified" when none), state (Running / Stopped / Fault / Changeover / Unknown), source (Manual / Tag / Alarm), confirmed (Yes/No) and actions.
6. Row actions: "Edit" and "Delete" show with control permission for the line, and unconfirmed events also show "Confirm"; after conditions change these buttons are temporarily disabled to prevent changing the stale list. Pages hold 50 rows.

■ How to use it
1. Choose the line and time range and click "Query". Once the hint disappears and the list times and lines match the filter, start working.
2. Adding downtime: click "Add", choose a line (it cannot be changed after the start), enter the start time; if the event has not ended, tick "Event still running" and leave the end empty; enter the state (Stopped / Fault / Changeover), reason and note, tick "Confirmed" as appropriate and save. After the list refreshes, check the start time, duration and reason.
3. Editing an existing event: click "Edit"; start and end time, state, reason, note and confirmation state can be changed. Clearing "Event still running" lets you add an end time. After saving, check that the duration stops growing.
4. Confirming events: click "Confirm" on rows whose confirmed value is No, and the list refreshes on success. Classifying the reason before confirming an unclassified event is recommended.
5. Output correction: click "Output correction", choose the line, enter the start and end time and the increase or decrease for good, defective and scrap quantities, enter a reason and save. Enter the amount to add or deduct; the list is queried again on success. Return to OEE and query again to check output and scrap rate.
6. Deleting an erroneous record: click "Delete" and confirm; the list refreshes on success.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. A query reports "Select a valid time range of no more than 366 days": the start is empty, the end is earlier than the start, or the span exceeds 366 days. Narrow the range and query again; parameters carried in from the OEE page pass the same check.
2. The table is capped at 2000 records: this is the display limit, not the number of events that exist. Narrow the time range or specify a line as prompted and query the rest.
3. "Duration (minutes)" keeps growing: the end time is empty and the event is treated as still running. Add an end time when editing, or clear that tick and save.
4. "Edit / Confirm / Delete" or "Add / Output correction" are missing: adding and output correction need at least one controllable line, and row buttons follow control permission for the line's area. Ask someone with control permission for that area to handle it.
5. Saving reports "Select a line", or parameters carried in from the OEE page report a line/range error: the line is empty, outside the controllable set, or the carried parameters are invalid. Select the line and time again before operating.
productionEvents.summary: Record downtime, classify reasons, confirm events and correct output for daily production.
productionEvents.title: Production events

project.body:
■ What this page is for
Project management works on the whole configuration: it stores configuration as version snapshots, can compare differences and roll back to older versions, and can export a project package for import into another system. It suits taking a baseline before and after major changes, or copying configuration between systems; it requires configure permission for any area. Project packages reference objects by name and contain no database IDs; after offline editing, preview the differences under Import & publish and publish once; publishing, rollback and screen publishing automatically take config snapshots, and operations are filtered by area permission and audited.

■ What is on the page
1. Top right: "Export project" exports a project package according to current permissions.
2. Version snapshots tab: a snapshot note box (up to 200 characters) and "Take snapshot"; on the right, "Compare" lets you choose the start and target versions (default "Current configuration", or a historical version).
3. Snapshot list: version, type (manual, import, before/after rollback and so on), note, creation time and creator, content and actions. "Roll back to here" is visible with configure permission; "Download" only with global configure permission.
4. Difference table: "Differences:" plus the start and end versions, a summary of added, overwritten, skipped and deleted counts at the top, and errors and insufficient permissions listed. Each row expands to show old and new values, with columns category, object, action, area and changed fields. Categories include areas, devices, tags, symbol library, screens and recipes. When part of the configuration is outside your permissions, " · X more outside your permissions" appears.
5. Import & publish: file box (.json), "Default conflict handling" (Skip, Overwrite, Import with rename), "Preview differences" and "Publish import". Once selected, the package name and exporter appear; the difference table gains a "Conflict handling" column, where each row can be changed and the preview refreshes automatically. "Publish import" requires a preview with no errors, no permission gaps and at least one non-skipped change.
6. Rollback dialog: titled "Roll back to configuration version #N", it states the impact as additions, overwrites and deletions, that deleting a tag ends its active alarms but keeps its history, and that a snapshot is taken automatically before the rollback. At the bottom are "Cancel" and the red "Confirm rollback", disabled when the preview has errors, permission gaps or no entries.

■ How to use it
1. Before making changes, write a note and click "Take snapshot"; an empty note shows "Enter a snapshot note", success shows "Snapshot #N created", and a new manual version appears in the list.
2. Reading differences: choose the start version on the left and "Current configuration" on the right, click "Compare", and expand entries to check old and new values; a permission hint means part of the content is hidden and a colleague with global configure permission should check it.
3. Rollback: click "Roll back to here" to review the impact preview; note that deleting tags affects active alarms. Click "Confirm rollback" and, after "Roll back N configuration items to version #X?", run it; success shows "Rolled back; version #N created". Verify: an "After rollback" version appears, comparing it with the target version is empty, and a "Before rollback" snapshot was created.
4. Export: click "Export project" to download the package and note the time for later checks; failure shows "Export failed".
5. Import: choose a package; an invalid file shows "The file is not a valid project package JSON". The system previews automatically; adjust conflict handling and preview again.
6. Publish import: click "Publish import"; after "Publish import of N changes? Any failure rolls back everything", click "Publish". Success shows "Published; version #N created"; failure shows "Import failed; everything was rolled back" and previews again. Verify: an import record is added to the version list and, compared with the pre-import snapshot, the differences should match the chosen handling.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. Rollback overwrites the current configuration and cannot be undone. Take a snapshot or export the project first; the automatically created "Before rollback" snapshot has a fixed note and is hard to identify later, so taking your own with a note is safer.
2. An import must be previewed first. Skip writes nothing, Overwrite replaces existing objects directly, and Import with rename adds objects under new names; choosing the wrong handling changes the field configuration and becomes the new baseline.
3. An import is one transaction and "any failure rolls back everything"; do not close the page while publishing. On failure, read the errors in the difference area, fix them and preview again.
4. Project packages reference by name and match by name across systems; objects with the same name but different meaning are easily overwritten. "Partial export by permission" means the permissions are incomplete and it cannot be treated as a full backup.
5. Version snapshots store configuration only, without history data or reports; for data backups together, use Operations & HA.
project.summary: Back up, compare and roll back the whole configuration, or import it into another system.
project.title: Project management

quality.body:
■ What this page is for
Quality analysis turns inspection records into yield trends and defect distribution. Inspectors record Passed, Failed, Rework or Scrap results here; managers spot slipping yield and the dominant defect types on the dashboard. Records are entered manually on this page; for a single unit's full history, follow its SN to Production traceability. Built for inspectors, quality engineers and shop-floor managers.

■ What is on the page
1. Three tabs: Inspections, Quality dashboard and Defect codes. “Refresh” reloads only the current tab.
2. Inspections: the last 7 days by default; search by SN, batch, product or inspector; filter by result, defect code, area and time range; 50 rows per page. An SN links to traceability; records with a linked tag offer “View trend” (±10 minutes around the inspection).
3. Quality dashboard: last 7/30/90 days, filterable by area, product and batch; cards for inspected count, yield, defect rate and scrap rate, plus a yield trend, a defect Pareto and a by-device table.
4. The math: yield = passed ÷ total; defect rate = (failed + rework + scrap) ÷ total; scrap rate = scrap ÷ total. The Pareto counts only non-passed records, grouped by defect code.
5. Defect codes: code, name, category, description and an enabled flag. Disabled codes are not offered during entry; codes referenced by records cannot be deleted.
6. Permissions: recording needs Control on the area; editing and deleting records and managing the dictionary need Configure. Buttons you cannot use are hidden.

■ How to use it
1. Build the dictionary: add defect codes (such as scratch or out-of-tolerance) under Defect codes, with categories as needed.
2. Record an inspection: “Record inspection” on the records tab; fill in SN, batch, product, area and result. Non-passed results require a defect code; link a device and tag to enable the trend look-back.
3. Read the trend: switch to the dashboard and pick the window; when yield dips, check which defect dominates the Pareto.
4. Drill down: click a Pareto bar to jump back to records filtered by that defect and the dashboard window; click an SN for unit traceability.
5. Fix mistakes: edit or delete records (Configure required); the dashboard recalculates after each change.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. Non-passed records must carry a defect code or the save is rejected; switching back to Passed clears the code.
2. Inspection time cannot be in the future; for backdating, set the actual inspection time.
3. A defect code referenced by records cannot be deleted, only disabled; history and statistics stay intact.
4. Days are grouped in the server's local timezone — mind the boundary if the server runs in another zone.
5. A new record missing from the dashboard: the summary only covers the selected window, so backdated inspections need the matching range.
6. “View trend” appears only when a tag is linked; it opens the trends page at the inspection time ±10 minutes.
quality.summary: Record inspections and read yield and defect distribution: the trend shows change, the Pareto shows what to fix first.
quality.title: Quality analysis

realtime.body:
■ What this page is for
Realtime lists the values collected from field devices one by one, such as temperature, pressure, output and switch states. You can see what each tag reads right now, its quality, the last sample time, and whether it has active alarms. For writable tags you are allowed to write, you can check and then send a setpoint and confirm it by read-back. It suits inspection rounds, commissioning and instrument checks; when something looks wrong you can jump straight to the alarms page or trends. Viewers can only read; operators or engineers with Control permission for the area can write. The page receives changed values by push and also refreshes a full snapshot every 10 seconds as a fallback.

■ What is on the page
1. Top notices: separate messages appear when device or tag configuration fails to load, the live snapshot cannot be read, or linked alarms fail to load. When some samples are stale, a notice says how many tags have stale or unverified samples.
2. Filter bar: the device dropdown offers All devices or a single device; the search box matches tag name, description and device name; quality offers All qualities, Abnormal only or Good only; sorting offers Configuration order or Attention first; Clear filters appears when filters are set.
3. Connection and refresh: the label on the right shows the push state: Push connected, Push connecting, Push reconnecting or Push disconnected. Pause freezes the current readings and shows when they were paused, Resume restores updates and fetches one snapshot to catch up, and Refresh snapshot is unavailable while paused. The last snapshot verification time is shown below.
4. Result totals: shows how many points are listed, with abnormal points and linked active alarms marked by red labels. Abnormal counts follow the current device and search scope; tags with no value read do not count as abnormal.
5. Tag table: device, tag, value (with unit), quality, linked active alarms, latest sample, description and actions. A blank device shows Calculated tags; quality may be Unread, Good, Fault, Communication interrupted or Uncertain; samples older than the threshold are marked Unverified; the collection error appears in red below the description.
6. Row and value colours: rows with uncertain quality are light orange, rows with fault or communication interruption are light red, and values are coloured too, so problems stand out in a long table.
7. Actions column: Open screen appears when screens can be opened, and View trend appears with trend permission; both are ordinary links. When the tag is writable and you have Control permission for that device, Write value is the only primary action on the row. A writable tag without permission shows Viewer is read-only; a non-writable tag shows Read-only. Write value is unavailable while refresh is paused.
8. Write dialog: shows the current value, target value and range; Boolean tags use a Set (1) / Clear (0) switch and numeric tags use an input box. The range and current value are shown below; a warning appears when the reference sample is stale or its quality is not Good. Before submission the system checks limits, interlocks, tag-out and control ownership.
9. Command receipt: for commands needing asynchronous confirmation or going through a gateway, the receipt number, execution state and read-back value appear in the dialog or below the page.
10. Pagination: 100 tags per page, with the total and page buttons at the bottom.

■ How to use it
1. Inspection: select a device or type a tag name, set quality to Abnormal only and sorting to Attention first, then check sample times and error messages one by one. To see how a value changed, click View trend; the trends page opens with that tag selected.
2. Checking readings: when values change too fast, click Pause; the page freezes at the current readings and shows the pause time, which is convenient for screenshots or checking. When done, click Resume: the system fetches one snapshot, so changes made while paused are not lost.
3. Writing: click Write value, check the current value and range, enter the target value and click Send. Boolean tags accept only set or clear, and integer tags do not accept decimals. If a confirmation box appears, check the current value, target value, limits, feedback condition, device mode (Local/Remote) and tag-out information before confirming. On success the page reports Written, read-back {value} and the value column updates.
4. Viewing linked alarms: click the count in the linked active alarms column to open the alarms page filtered by that tag and by active, suppressed or shelved state. Without alarm permission the column shows Not authorized only.
5. Handling stale samples: first read the error under the description and the latest sample time, then judge together with the device communication state. When a whole device is offline, test the connection or open collection diagnostics on the device configuration page.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. "Enter a valid value within the configured range. Integer points do not accept decimals." means the target is outside the tag's configured limits, or you entered a decimal for an integer tag. Adjust the value and submit again.
2. A failed write with a rejection reason means the server check found an exceeded limit, too fast a rate of change, an unmet interlock, a tag-out on the device or Local mode. Resolve the field condition first; do not resubmit the same command repeatedly.
3. "Submitted for dual approval; waiting for another user to approve" or "This operation keeps the original command ID" means the command has entered approval or receipt processing. Check the result in the command receipt instead of reopening the dialog and submitting again, which would send it twice.
4. An Unverified sample time can mean the snapshot read failed, no successful refresh for more than 30 seconds, or a long sampling interval (the threshold is the larger of 30 seconds and three collection cycles). Investigate using the error under the description and the connection state.
5. If a tag cannot be found, search matches name, description and device name, so clear the device filter or switch back to All qualities and search again; if it still does not appear, you have no view permission for that tag. No data updates while refresh is paused and a greyed-out write button are both normal.
realtime.summary: See the current value of every tag like reading a thermometer, and safely write setpoints when needed.
realtime.title: Realtime

recipes.body:
■ What this page is for
Recipe management stores the temperatures, pressures, times and other parameters a machine needs for different products as recipes, then downloads the whole batch to the device. It suits product changeovers, trial runs and restoring standard process parameters. It shares the same control loop as field control: before download all parameters are pre-checked together (control ownership, tag-out, limits, rate of change, permissives, recipe limits), and only if all pass are they written one by one and verified by read-back; whole-batch dual approval applies when required. Process engineers and configuration administrators build templates and edit recipes; operators and shift leaders download and review. Opening this page requires view permission for at least one area, editing requires Configure permission, and download and abort require Control permission. A recipe configured for whole-batch dual approval goes to "Field control → Pending approval" after submission until approved.

■ What is on the page
1. Top: a hint describing the download flow and a Refresh button.
2. Recipes tab: search box (name, description or parameter), template filter, Clear, New recipe, Upload from field as new recipe (select a template first), and a Showing X / Y records count.
3. Recipe table: recipe (name, template name · version, description and View downloads), parameters (first 3 shown, expandable via "N more parameters"), last modified (person, time, note) and actions.
4. Actions column: Download appears with Control permission and Edit with Configure permission; More contains Copy recipe, Version history, Compare with field, Upload and Delete.
5. Download log area: a strip for the latest submission stating "Showing the latest 200 download records. Pending and running records update every second"; search by ID, recipe or operator, and filter by recipe and status (All statuses, Pending / Running, Failed / Rejected / Aborted, Completed).
6. Download record table: download (#ID recipe version), status (Pending approval, Running, Completed, Failed, Partially downloaded, Aborted, Rejected), parameters (status label, parameter name, before → target value, read-back value, message) and execution (requester, reviewer, time, message); running records offer Abort.
7. Download confirmation dialog: shows the recipe name and version and "Pre-checking. Please wait for the result…" while checking; the table lists parameter, tag, current → target and check (Passed or the rejection reason); Dual approval required appears when review is needed, and Confirm download becomes Submit for approval for dual approval.
8. Recipe edit: template (cannot be changed when editing an existing recipe), name (up to 100 characters), description (up to 500 characters), a number box per parameter (showing unit, range [low limit, high limit] and tag) and version note (up to 200 characters), with Load live values, Cancel and Save at the bottom; when editing, the title shows the version number that saving will create.
9. Versions and comparison: version history lists version, source (Edit/Upload/Project), values, change and Compare with current; the comparison dialog shows "{left} ↔ {right}: {N} differences", with columns parameter, Left, Right and Different; differing rows are highlighted.
10. Templates tab: searchable, with New template; the table lists template, area, parameters (name, tag, unit, [low limit, high limit]), review and edit/delete; the template dialog has name, area, description and dual approval for the whole batch, and the parameter table can add and remove rows (key, name, tag, unit, low limit, high limit).

■ How to use it
1. Build a template: click New template, select the area, fill in name and description, tick Dual approval for the whole batch if needed, click Add parameter to select a tag and fill in key, name, unit and limits, then save; Saved confirms it.
2. Create a recipe: click New recipe, select the template and fill in name and description; parameters are pre-filled with defaults or low limits and can be edited by hand, or click Load live values to fill in field values (only tags with Good quality). Saving shows Saved as new version.
3. Download: click Download, wait for the pre-check, check each current → target row and its check result, then click Confirm download. The message "Submitted; another authorized user must approve under Field control → Pending approval" means dual approval; otherwise the page reports Start download #ID. Check the read-back values in the download log; the download only succeeded when the status is Completed.
4. Changing parameters: click Edit; saving creates a new version. To compare against the field first, use Compare with field under More, then download.
5. Upload: select a template, click Upload from field as new recipe and enter a name, or click Upload under More on a row and enter a version note, to save the tags' current values as a new recipe or a new version.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. When the pre-check fails the confirm button is grey and the page reports "Some parameters failed checks; the batch cannot be downloaded (it is never partially downloaded)." with the reasons; typical causes are exceeding recipe limits, tag-out, Local mode or exceeded limits. Fix them and run the check again.
2. A Partially downloaded record means a parameter failed to write and the download stopped immediately; values already written are not rolled back or resent automatically. Confirm the field state manually before proceeding.
3. "The pre-check does not match the current recipe or version. Run the check again." means the recipe was edited or its version changed during the check; click Run pre-check again and resubmit.
4. Parameter inputs are already limited by the template limits, so out-of-range values cannot be entered; after lowering template limits, existing recipes may fall outside the range and must be corrected manually.
5. Abort stops only unfinished writes; parameters already written are not rolled back. Load live values fills only valid values and keeps the rest unchanged, reporting "No live value for N parameters; kept existing values".
recipes.summary: Package a set of process parameters as a recipe and send the whole batch to devices when needed.
recipes.title: Recipe management

reportCenter.body:
■ What this page is for
Business reports generate shift, daily or monthly reports from templates, archive them as Excel and PDF, and support file integrity checks, electronic signatures and review with approval. Unlike the temporary Tag statistics query, a template here binds an area, a period and column definitions; a generated archive cannot be modified, and regenerating the same period creates a new version and keeps the old one. Maintaining templates requires Configure permission for the corresponding area. The archive list only shows reports from templates the current account can access.

■ What is on the page
1. Top: the title "Business reports", with Tag statistics and Refresh on the right; a hint beside the template title explains that templates are granted by area, archives are Excel and PDF and cannot be modified, regenerating the same period creates a new version, and SHA256 is verified on download.
2. View switch: Generated archives and Templates & generation.
3. Template table: template (name, period · area · revision), columns (each column title), schedule / email (n minutes after period end or not sent, recipients) and actions (History, Generate previous period, Edit, Copy template, Delete; all except History require Configure permission for that area).
4. Archive table: filterable by template; columns cover history report lookup (template name, revision, period key), generation time (trigger, generator, cleanup label), signature / approval (signed or unsigned; Pending review / Reviewed; Pending approval / Approved / Rejected) and actions (View, Excel, PDF, Verify / sign).
5. View dialog: the first column is Period, column headers carry units, values follow the configured decimals, and a total row appears at the end.
6. Verify / sign dialog: shows the verification result, certificate subject and fingerprint; the file table lists format, SHA256 (Match / Mismatch / Missing), digital signature state and Download .p7s; an external copy can be uploaded for comparison, and the approval and signing form is shown.
7. Template editor: name, period, area, shift start, scheduled generation and delay, email channel and recipients; column definitions include key, title, type, tag or job, factor, decimals and unit; Add column, batch add and KPI presets are at the bottom.

■ How to use it
1. Maintain a template: switch to Templates & generation, click New report template and fill in name, period and area; turn on Scheduled generation and set the delay in minutes for automatic generation; for email, select an email channel and enter recipients.
2. Configure columns: click Add column to set each column, or click Batch add tag columns to select several tags and Average, Maximum, Minimum; KPI presets add common metrics; after saving, check the period, area and column titles.
3. Generate: click Generate previous period on a template row; the confirmation shows the number of existing archives. After confirming, the page reports "Generated {period} v{revision}" and the list switches to that template.
4. View and download: click View on an archive row to check the data; click Excel or PDF to download. The buttons are unavailable when the file has been deleted by the retention policy.
5. Verify and sign: click Verify / sign. When verification passes and the state is Pending review / Reviewed, Pending approval, the review or approval form appears; choose approve or reject, enter a reason and password, then submit. At the bottom you can optionally check a local file; it either matches with a valid signature or reports a mismatch.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. If verification fails or the report shows Unsigned: on failure the page warns "Verification failed: the file or signature record may have been tampered with" or SHA256 shows Mismatch / Missing; do not use the file, and first check its source and version. Unsigned means signing was not enabled or failed at generation; the signature download and approval cannot continue.
2. A failed signature clears the password box: the password was wrong, you lack permission, or the step has already been handled. Approval requires Configure permission for the area and must differ from the reviewer; a reason is required.
3. "Select an area you can configure" on save means the template area must be within the areas the current account can configure.
4. Formula, difference and accumulate columns have fixed definitions: formulas may only reference earlier columns (written as $key); Difference is end-of-period minus start-of-period, and a falling reading is treated as a meter reset; Accumulate is a time-weighted integral and gaps over 1 hour are not bridged; the total row recomputes or sums over the whole period.
5. Deleting a template deletes only the template; archived reports are kept. Regenerating the same period appends a new version and keeps the old one; after changing the template, confirm the definitions used by the new version.
reportCenter.summary: Generate formal reports from templates, archive and download them, verify signatures and run review/sign-off.
reportCenter.title: Business reports

screenDesigner.body:
■ What this page is for
The screen designer is the workbench for building process screens. Components, symbols and layers are on the left, the canvas in the middle and the properties panel on the right. Drag pumps, valves, meters and other elements (small parts on the screen) onto the canvas, set their position and size, then bind tags (a data point on a device) so they show real values, state colours and alarms at runtime. Save the finished screen as a draft, then publish; only after publishing can the field see it in Screen runtime and the runtime workbench. The main users are administrators with global Configure permission; operators do not enter this page.

■ What is on the page
1. Top toolbar: screen list, open or return to runtime, screen name input (up to 100 characters), Saved / Unsaved label, Draft rX / published rY, Undo, Redo, Validate, Preview, publication history, Save draft and Publish.
2. Components and layers on the left: component search showing "Showing X / Y items"; industrial elements (text, value, pump, valve, meter, button, switch, chart and so on, dragged or clicked to add); ISA-101 symbol library (mostly grayscale, status colours only for running/alarm); user symbols; templates / faceplates (with placeholder counts); a layer list that can be searched, locked, hidden and reordered by dragging.
3. Canvas in the middle: zoom, Fit canvas, Locate selection, Snap to grid, Save as template, Arrange menu (align, match size, distribute evenly), group/ungroup, Lock selection, Hide selection, Copy, Move up, Move down and Delete.
4. Properties panel on the right: Basics and style, Data, Element settings and Interaction. The data section binds tags and sets unit, range, decimals and state mapping; control elements must bind a writable tag and select Control write; text elements set text, font size and alignment, and shape elements set colour, border and corner radius.
5. Validate, publish and history: Validate opens Screen check results listing issues such as a tag that no longer exists, a control without a writable tag, an unpublished navigation target, a chart with more than 12 tags, or a font size or decimals value out of range; publication history shows versions and supports rollback; on a save conflict you can Load server version or Keep local and overwrite.
6. Local backup and templates: unsaved content is cached in this browser, and on re-entry the page reports "Unsaved local draft found" with Restore local draft or Discard this backup; Save as template packages the selected elements into a template with placeholders.

■ How to use it
1. Click Edit in the screen list to open this page and confirm the top shows Draft rX / published rY.
2. Search on the left or drag elements onto the canvas; drag an element to move it and drag its bottom-right handle to resize; use Arrange for precise alignment.
3. Select an element and bind its tag on the right, then set unit, range and decimals; for state lights, pumps and valves also configure state mapping, and for buttons configure the action or control write.
4. Click Validate and fix the issues one by one; then click Preview to confirm the appearance. Preview never sends control commands.
5. Click Save draft to write to the server; Publish saves the changes first, then opens the publication impact confirmation; if published layouts or workstations use the screen, their names are listed and publishing waits for confirmation.
6. After publishing, return to the screen list or runtime and refresh to confirm the new version is active.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. "Save rejected: N issue(s)" or "Publish rejected" means server validation failed and the issues are listed in Screen check results; fix them and save or publish again instead of clicking repeatedly.
2. Save conflict means the server draft advanced to a higher revision, so someone else has edited it; review the differences and decide whether to load the server version or overwrite, since no automatic merge occurs.
3. "The screen has unsaved changes. Leave anyway?" means leaving discards unsaved changes; save the draft first or confirm leaving. The browser keeps a local backup but never writes it to the server automatically.
4. If the save or publish button does not respond, it is disabled while saving, loading, or after a read failure; refresh and retry. A screen holds at most 1000 elements; split a larger one.
5. If a control does nothing at runtime, the control element has no writable tag, its tag was deleted, the account lacks Control permission, or the device is Local or tagged out; run Validate before publishing to catch binding problems.
screenDesigner.summary: Place widgets, bind tags and build equipment process screens like assembling blocks.
screenDesigner.title: Screen designer

screenRun.body:
■ What this page is for
Screen runtime opens and runs a single published process screen. It is especially useful on multi-monitor industrial PCs: one monitor shows the overview and another shows equipment screens. It differs from the runtime workbench, which assembles several screens in a grid; Screen runtime handles one screen and can open the same screen again in a new window on a chosen monitor. Field operators use it daily; clicking Run in the process screen list opens this page with the screen ID in the address.

■ What is on the page
1. Top toolbar: Back to screens on the left returns to the process screen list with the previous filters kept; Open in new window beside it places the screen on a chosen monitor.
2. Screen toolbar: screen name, connection state (Live, or a warning-colored Reconnecting · snapshot refresh) and More. More opens Screen options: the runtime version (such as Runtime version 3), System active alarms when the screen uses alarms, screen zoom (Fit or 50% to 150%), Refresh, and Edit current screen when you have global Configure permission and are not in monitor mode. Draft preview, monitor mode and mobile read-only are labeled beside the name.
3. Monitor selection dialog: after clicking Open in new window, the monitors the browser can see are listed, each with a name and width×height; select one and click Open to run the same screen in a new window named after the screen ID.
4. Runtime area: shows the published screen's elements, live values, alarm states and operable controls; on a read-only mobile client or when the account lacks Control permission, control buttons are disabled or report no permission when clicked.
5. Version and error notices: when runtime detects a new published version it reports "A newer publication rX is available. Reload to apply it." with Reload; failures to load the screen, live values, alarms or history are shown in a notice strip.

■ How to use it
1. In the process screen list, confirm the screen is published and click Run to open this page.
2. Check the connection state on the screen toolbar. The runtime version is inside More, under Screen options, and confirms the latest published version is open.
3. To use a second screen, click Open in new window, select the target monitor in the dialog and click Open; the browser tries to move the window to that monitor's position and open it at its size.
4. To change the display size, open More and choose Fit or a percentage under Screen options. When values stop updating, click Refresh in the same place to reload the screen and live values.
5. To change the screen, open More and click Edit current screen under Screen options. After saving and publishing, return here, click Reload on the notice, then open More again to confirm the version number changed.
6. When finished, click Back to screens.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. "The browser blocked the new window; allow popups for this site" means the window was blocked and did not open; allow popups for this site and retry, or view it in the current window.
2. If the monitor list shows only Current monitor, or the window did not move to the second screen, the browser does not support window management or the user denied monitor permission; the system falls back to a regular new window that must be dragged to the target monitor. Some browsers also ignore window position arguments.
3. Opening on the wrong screen: with several monitors the second is selected by default, and with only one the single item is selected; before opening, confirm the detected monitor name and resolution.
4. If a control button does nothing, controls are disabled on a read-only mobile client or because the account lacks Control permission; the server also rejects writes when the device is tagged out, in Local mode or outside the range. Do not bypass these limits.
5. If the page reports a new published version but nothing changed, runtime switches only after you click Reload and never interrupts the current operation automatically.
screenRun.summary: Choose a monitor and open a published process screen in a new window.
screenRun.title: Screen runtime

screens.body:
■ What this page is for
Process screens are the equipment dashboards field operators look at. A screen usually contains equipment drawings, live values, state lights, buttons and alarm hints, bringing the key information of a line or a device together on one page. This page is the screen list: it does not draw screens but manages the catalog of all screens, showing which are published, which are drafts, which have been changed but not published, and how many runtime layouts use them. Actual drawing happens in the screen designer, and only after publishing can a screen be opened in Screen runtime, the runtime workbench and other field pages. The main users are configuration administrators; ordinary operators only see published screens.

■ What is on the page
1. Top toolbar: administrators with global Configure permission see New screen; everyone sees Refresh. A hint icon beside the title explains "Drafts are visible to administrators only; published screens run in the field".
2. Filters: "Search screen name or editor" accepts several space-separated words and shows only screens matching all of them; administrators can also filter by All statuses, Published, Not published or Unpublished changes; sorting offers Recently updated or Name; Clear filters appears when filters are set; "Showing X of Y screens" is shown on the right.
3. Screen cards: screen name, status label (Published / Draft / has unpublished changes), editor and modification time, published and draft revisions; when referenced by layouts, "Used in N runtime layout(s)" is also shown.
4. Action buttons: Preview opens the screen read-only in a dialog; Run opens it on the screen run page; Create workbench from this screen quickly creates a runtime workbench; administrators also find Edit, Duplicate and Delete in the More menu.
