5. Empty states: with no screens the page says "Create your first process screen, bind device tags, then publish"; with no matches it says "No screens match your filters" and offers Clear filters; on a load failure it shows the error and Reload.

■ How to use it
1. First confirm whether the screen is published. Drafts are visible to administrators only and never appear in field runtime; when a card shows Not published or Unpublished changes, publish it from the designer.
2. To see the result, click Preview and check the layout, values and states in the dialog; preview never executes controls.
3. To show it in the field, click Run, then choose a monitor on the screen run page to place it on a second screen.
4. To modify it, click Edit under More to open the screen designer; click Validate, fix issues, Save draft, then Publish. Coming back to this page and clicking Refresh should show Published with a higher revision.
5. For a new screen, click New screen, enter a name of 1 to 100 characters in the prompt and confirm; the designer opens directly.
6. For a combined presentation, click Create workbench from this screen, choose the presentation, preview and publish as prompted; success opens the runtime workbench.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. "Enter 1–100 characters" means the new screen name is empty or longer than 100 characters; shorten it and retry. Leading and trailing spaces are removed.
2. If the Run button does not appear, it is shown only when the screen has a published version; when unpublished changes exist, runtime uses the last published version, so publish first.
3. The delete prompt "It is also removed from runtime screens" means deletion also removes the screen from runtime; when a card shows "Used in N runtime layout(s)", check those layouts first to avoid empty regions.
4. If a screen cannot be found, search matches both screen name and editor and all keywords must match; click Clear filters to reset.
5. On a read or action failure the page keeps the original error; click Refresh or Reload first. If it keeps failing, check the service connection and the account's global Configure permission; the front end only hides entry points, and server-side checks are authoritative.
screens.summary: Manage the screens operators see: preview, run, edit, copy and publish them.
screens.title: Process screens

spc.body:
■ What this page is for
Statistical process control samples a tag on a fixed interval, plots mean and range control charts, and flags abnormal variation with run rules. Limits are established automatically and violations raise alarms, so process and quality engineers can watch critical characteristics. Only numeric tags qualify (no Bool), the tag must belong to the selected area, and only Good-quality values are sampled.

■ What is on the page
1. Toolbar: chart selector and time range (2 hours to 7 days). The page refreshes every 30 seconds, paused while the edit dialog is open.
2. Summary line: tag, chart type, sample count, active violation flags, and the latest mean, range, Cp and Cpk.
3. Two charts: mean and range, with dashed UCL/CL/LCL lines; red “Out” marks flag violating samples.
4. Rule violations table: time, rule, message, Active/Recovered; the alarm number links to that alarm on the alarms page.
5. Five run rules, selectable per chart: beyond the 3-sigma limit, 2 of 3 points beyond 2 sigma, 4 of 5 points beyond 1 sigma, 8 consecutive points on one side, range beyond the control limit.
6. Limits and specs: automatic limits use the first N subgroups as the baseline, showing “Limits are provisional x/N” until full; or switch auto off and enter CL/UCL/LCL. Spec USL/LSL drive capability: both sides give Cp and Cpk, one side gives Cpk only.

■ How to use it
1. Add a chart: “Add chart”, pick area and tag. Individuals and moving range (I-MR) suits single readings; mean and range (Xbar-R) groups readings into subgroups.
2. Set the sampling: interval in seconds and baseline subgroups; Xbar-R also needs a subgroup size (2–10) — one sample is produced per full subgroup.
3. Pick rules and specs: all five rules default to on; fill in spec limits to see Cp/Cpk.
4. Let the baseline build: automatic limits freeze once the baseline subgroups are collected; until then the provisional limits shift with each sample while rules stay active.
5. Work the violations: check red marks and Active rows, follow the alarm number to acknowledge; violations and alarms recover automatically when the process does.
6. Re-baseline the chart: after a process change, “Reset limits” starts a fresh baseline from new samples.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. No samples at all: only Good-quality numeric values count — if the device is offline or quality is bad, check the tag in Realtime first.
2. Violations are alarms: beyond 3σ raises a Critical alarm, other rules a Warning; they end on recovery, and disabling or deleting the chart ends its active alarms too.
3. Changing the sampling resets history: tag, chart type, subgroup size, interval, baseline subgroups or the auto-limits switch start a new generation — old samples disappear and limits rebuild. Renaming, description, rules or spec edits keep history.
4. Cp/Cpk shows “-”: no spec limits, or limits not yet established. Cp needs both spec sides; a one-sided spec yields Cpk only.
5. The charts load at most the latest 2000 samples and 200 violations per query — shorten the range for more detail.
6. Concurrent edits are rejected with “modified, refresh and retry”; editing, deleting and resetting require Configure on the chart's area.
spc.summary: Watch key tags for process drift: automatic sampling, rule violations with alarms, and Cp/Cpk capability.
spc.title: SPC control charts

system.body:
■ What this page is for
System administration is the administrator back office for accounts, permissions, auditing and health: managing users and area grants, resetting passwords, checking the operation log, maintaining areas and roles, and reviewing run state and storage usage. Opening the page requires User management, System maintenance or global Configure permission; tabs then follow permissions: User management needs User management permission, Operation log and System status need System maintenance permission, and Areas and roles needs User management or Configure permission.

■ What is on the page
1. User management: the table lists ID, user name, display name, role, status and actions; actions are Edit, Area grants, Reset password and Delete (not yourself). The user dialog has user name (up to 32 characters, not editable when editing), initial password (new users only), display name, role and Enable; Reset password only asks for a new password.
2. Area grants dialog: choose a role and area row by row (leave the area empty for all areas), with add and remove; built-in roles apply to all areas and custom roles add on top.
3. Operation log: query by time range and keyword. The table has time, operator, action, tag, previous value, new value, change details and result; coloured labels distinguish Success, Failed, Denied and so on; page size can be 20, 50, 100 or 200 rows.
4. Areas and roles: the area table has ID, name, description and device count, and the default area cannot be deleted; the role table has name, permission labels and grant count, and a role with grants cannot be deleted. Permissions are view, control, alarm acknowledgement, configure, user management and system maintenance.
5. System status: an "Auto-refresh every 10 s" hint. Six cards show run state, running time, online devices and tag count, data bus backlog, and disk and historical data usage.
6. History data and capacity: lists total usage, available space, raw and aggregate history databases, spool files, average daily net growth, estimated days to the warning threshold, retention and query concurrency; capacity warnings appear in yellow.
7. Device status table: device, status, last poll, collection period, tag count, reconnects, failures and errors.

■ How to use it
1. Create an account: enter user name (at least 3 characters), initial password (at least 6 characters) and display name, choose a role and whether to enable, then save. If "No global role (area grants only)" is selected, also click Area grants to add roles and areas, otherwise the account has no area to work in.
2. Adjust permissions: use Edit to change the role; to grant only certain areas, click Area grants, add rows and save. To verify, log in again and confirm only data from granted areas is visible.
3. Reset a password: enter a new password of at least 6 characters and confirm; the page reports Password reset.
4. Disable and delete: turning off Enable disables the account, which can no longer log in but keeps its configuration and logs; deleting asks you to confirm "Delete user {name}?" and reports Deleted on success.
5. Audit query: choose a time range, enter a keyword and click Query. Narrow the range first, then use the result labels to find anomalies and click Change details to check previous and new values.
6. Areas and roles: to create an area, enter name and description; after saving the table shows the device count. To create a role, tick permissions and save. The default area cannot be deleted, and a role with grants must have them removed first.
7. Watch capacity and check devices: review free disk, history usage and net growth together with retention to judge whether to add space; Incomplete scan means the statistics have not finished. Use Communication failed and Reconnects in the device table to find problem devices.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. A user name shorter than 3 characters reports "User name must be at least 3 characters", and a password shorter than 6 characters reports "Password must be at least 6 characters"; nothing is saved. Resetting a password also requires at least 6 characters.
2. Roles have two layers: Administrator, Operator and Viewer are built-in and apply to all areas; custom roles are granted per area. Selecting "No global role (area grants only)" without adding area grants leaves the account with no visible data after login.
3. Deleting an account cannot be undone and asks for confirmation only once; logs are kept but the account disappears. To block login temporarily, disable the account instead.
4. "Waiting for the gateway receipt" and "Failed, result unconfirmed" are neither success nor failure: no final receipt was received. Verify the actual state in Realtime and do not resend the command.
5. Capacity figures come from a scheduled scan and may show Incomplete scan. Fast growth usually means too short a collection period or too small a deadband; review tag storage modes and deadbands before adding space.
system.summary: Manage users, inspect audit logs and check runtime health and history storage.
system.title: System administration

tags.body:
■ What this page is for
A tag is the smallest unit the collection system knows on a device, such as Boiler 1 temperature or Line A01 output. Tag configuration tells the system where the data lives on the device and at which address, which type to read, whether to scale it, whether to store history and whether writing is allowed. Without tags a connected device is an empty shell; with a wrong address, Realtime shows bad quality or no value. Commissioning, device expansion and bulk copying of similar points all happen here, and the page also links to alarm rules, calculated tags and calculation jobs. Opening this page requires Configure permission for any area.

■ What is on the page
1. Filters: the device dropdown can be cleared and typed into, and the search box matches tag name or description; after changing conditions click Query, otherwise the page notes that the previous result is still shown. Clear filters, Refresh and a calculated tags link are also here. Above the table, the total result count and an Engineering columns switch (off by default) are shown.
2. Tool buttons: Byte order preview (the dialog is titled Byte order / address preview), Export Excel, Import Excel, Batch create tags and Add tag. Import Excel is shown only to accounts with global Configure permission. Selecting rows reveals Selected N, Batch archive and Batch delete.
3. List: common columns are device, tag name (with an alarm rules link below), address, type, unit, writable and storage; turning on Engineering columns adds ID, description, area, scale/offset and deadband. In the address column, calculated tags show their expression, derived tags show the job output, and S7 shows the DB number and bit offset. 100 rows per page, sortable by name or ID. For a physical tag, Edit is the primary action, and Configure alarms, Copy and Delete are under More. A calculated tag's primary action is Calculation definition, and a derived tag's is Job; those rows have no More menu.
4. Form: device, tag name (1 to 100 characters), description, area, address, data type, scale factor, offset, unit, storage mode, deadband, period (seconds), minimum, maximum and Allow write. OPC UA uses a NodeId, text protocols use a text address, S7 data blocks also need the DB number, and Boolean tags also need a bit offset.
5. Batch creation dialog: device, area, start address, count, step, name prefix, start index, index digits, data type, unit, DB number, archive mode and writable, with a generated preview table below where names can be edited row by row.

■ How to use it
1. Select a device and click Query; confirm it is registered in device configuration and has passed a test before adding tags.
2. Click Add tag, choose the device, enter the name and select the area. The area switches with the protocol: Modbus defaults to holding registers, S7 to data blocks, OPC UA to OPC UA nodes. Enter the address and data type, and fill scale and offset when raw values must become engineering units.
3. Choose the storage mode: no storage for live viewing only; on-change storage for states and alarms; periodic storage for trends and reports, which requires a period greater than 0 seconds. A read-only area does not show Allow write and forces it off on save.
4. After saving, return to the list and use Byte order preview or the test read on the device page with the same area and address to check whether a sensible raw value is read.
5. Batch creation: set the start address, count, step and naming rule, check and rename rows in the preview, then click Create N tags. Afterwards refresh the list to confirm the count and addresses.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. "Address exceeds 65535" means start address plus (count minus 1) times step exceeds the limit. Reduce the count or lower the start address.
2. "Tag names are duplicated" means batch names are built from prefix plus index and too few index digits cause clashes. Change the prefix or increase the index digits.
3. "Periodic archive period must be greater than 0" means periodic storage is selected but the period is empty. Enter a positive integer and save again.
4. Messages such as "Select a device and enter the tag name", "Enter a NodeId" or "Enter an address" point to highlighted fields; fill them in, and remember OPC UA and text protocols always need an address.
5. If Import Excel is missing, importing can overwrite tags on any device and requires global Configure permission; with area permission only, add tags individually or use batch creation. After import, the page lists added, updated and skipped counts plus errors.
6. Deletion cannot be undone; calculated and derived tags cannot be deleted in tag configuration and must be removed on the calculated tags page and the calculation jobs page respectively, and deletion is refused while a calculated tag is referenced.
tags.summary: A tag is one data point on a device. Here you define its name, address, type and storage.
tags.title: Tag configuration

traceability.body:
■ What this page is for
Traceability answers who made this product, when, and whether it passed inspection. Each product is identified by an SN (serial number); when inspection is triggered the system captures a group of fields under that SN and reports Passed, Failed, Unknown or Not evaluated. It suits quality, process and after-sales staff investigating a product, and field staff binding a scanned SN. It relies on PLC devices from tag configuration and on the capture jobs on this page; a common pattern is to trigger capture by scanning, then look up values by SN when something is wrong.

■ What is on the page
1. Top: the title "Traceability" and a refresh button; refreshing reloads jobs and tags, and the scan tab shows the pending SN, expiry and reply.
2. Records: SN input (up to 200 characters), capture job, inspection result, time range and Search. Changed conditions are flagged; on failure the previous results are kept.
3. Record table: expand a row to see field name, captured value, unit and inspection result; the main row shows SN, job, inspection result, captured at and PLC acknowledgement (Replied 2 or Saved, awaiting reply). A note below explains that inspection results and acknowledgement are independent; records without configured evaluation show Not evaluated.
4. Scan Binding: the job dropdown lists only enabled jobs that are not PLC sources and accept scans. Web scan shows the SN input and Bind SN; the information area shows source, state, pending SN, expires at and reply value, with Clear pending SN when one is pending and a yellow warning on errors.
5. Capture Jobs: the table lists capture job, trigger point, SN source, enabled, state, scanner connection and edit; New job requires Configure and Control permission; whether a row can be edited depends on Configure and Control permission for that job's area.
6. Job dialog: name, enabled, PLC device, trigger point, SN source and the duplicate SN check; a PLC source needs the SN format and registers, a scanner source needs an expiry of 5 to 3600 seconds plus TCP or serial connection parameters. Below, capture fields (up to 64) and the inspection outcome mapping can be added.

■ How to use it
1. On Capture Jobs, create a job: select a PLC device (only devices the current account can configure and control are listed), select the trigger point (a writable point on that device with no Boolean type and scale 1, offset 0), then select the SN source.
2. Fill in parameters for the source: for PLC, choose the SN format (Numeric, ASCII low byte first or ASCII high byte first) and the registers; numeric format takes one register, ASCII takes several and only UInt16 points with scale 1 and offset 0. For a scanner, enter the expiry (300 seconds by default) and, for a serial scanner, the connection parameters.
3. Add capture fields: each needs a name and a data point; for automatic evaluation, select one result field under Inspection outcome mapping and enter the pass value and a different fail value. Before saving, confirm all required items are filled in.
4. After saving, go to Scan Binding, select the job, enter an SN and click Bind SN. Binding succeeded when Pending SN appears and Expires at shows the expiry time.
5. On Records, search by SN and expand a record to check fields, units, inspection result, captured at and PLC acknowledgement; after changing a job, refresh the list to check state and scanner connection.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. "Saved, awaiting reply" is not a failed inspection: the data is saved but the PLC handshake has not replied. Result and acknowledgement are separate; check the result first, then investigate the acknowledgement.
2. If Scan Binding has no jobs or an empty dropdown, only enabled jobs that are not PLC sources and accept scans are listed; check Enable and the source in Capture Jobs, then refresh.
3. While an SN is pending, the input and Bind SN are disabled: only one is allowed at a time, and you must wait for expiry or click Clear pending SN before binding again; the expiry is adjustable from 5 to 3600 seconds.
4. "Complete the job, trigger, SN source and data fields." on save means the name, trigger point or complete capture fields are missing; a PLC source also needs its registers.
5. "Select a valid result field and enter two distinct finite values." means the two values are equal or empty. Changing the PLC device clears the trigger point, registers and capture fields, and the mapping too; records without a mapping show Not evaluated, and upgrades never reclassify history.
6. Duplicate SN check is off by default: when enabled, the same SN captured by this job within the last 10 days is rejected with PLC reply 3, while other jobs and records older than 10 days are unaffected.

trends.body:
■ What this page is for
Trends draws historical tag values as line charts, like a temperature record, to show when a value changed, what it changed to and for how long. It suits fault review, shift handover comparisons and verifying the effect of a process change, and it can compare several tags over the same period. The curves come from archived history, not live values; to see the current value, use Realtime. When you arrive from the Trend button on the alarms page or View trend in Realtime, the tag ID is in the address and the page selects that tag and queries automatically.

■ What is on the page
1. Tag selection: searchable and multi-select, up to 50 tags at once; options are shown as device / tag to avoid confusing tags with the same name on different devices. "{n} selected" appears on the right, and Clear is available after selecting.
2. Time range: five presets (1 hour, 6 hours, 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days); clicking one immediately queries the period from that duration ago to now and highlights the button. You can also choose a start and end time, which queries automatically once selected; clearing the custom time returns to 1 hour.
3. Query and refresh: Query reloads the curves for the current conditions; turning on Auto refresh re-queries every 30 seconds, which suits watching a live process.
4. Result labels: Source shows Raw data, 5-minute aggregates or Hourly aggregates; when data exists it also shows "{n} points / {m} tags". The larger the range, the more likely the system aggregates or downsamples automatically.
5. Export: Export CSV saves the current result as a table with time, tag, value and quality. The button is unavailable when there is no data, when conditions changed without a new query, or while a query is running.
6. Chart area: tags with the same unit share a chart and scale, while different units use separate panels; Boolean tags use 0/1 step lines on raw data, and aggregates show the sample mean. Clicking a chart moves the playback cursor to that moment.
7. Playback bar: play / pause, back to start, a time slider and speed choices (1×, 10×, 60×, 300×). 1× is real time, the default is 60×, and 300× replays about 5 minutes of data per second. Below the cursor, each tag's value and quality at that moment are listed; hover to see the exact time.
8. History analysis: when the query has at most 20 tags and a span of no more than 24 hours, the history analysis table loads automatically with time-weighted average, minimum, maximum, integral (value·h), coverage, good quality samples and quality interval bands. Otherwise a notice states the limits.
9. Notices: the tag catalog can be reloaded after a load failure; separate notices cover a failed query, a tag in the address that does not exist or is not accessible, changed query conditions, and Boolean tags being aggregated or downsampled; the range and tag count of the displayed result also appear above the chart.
10. Empty states: with no tags selected, before a query, or when the period truly has no data, the chart area explains the situation instead of staying blank.

■ How to use it
1. Arriving from alarms: click Trend on an alarm row and the matching tag is selected automatically. Set the range around the alarm (for example 1 hour before to 1 hour after) and click Query to see how values changed before and after it.
2. Comparing several tags: add related tags in tag selection, up to 50. After querying, the same units share a chart and different units are separated; legend names include the device name for clarity.
3. Replaying a period: click play and the cursor advances at the chosen speed while the values below update; drag the slider or click the chart to jump to any moment; playback stops at the end, and Back to start begins again.
4. Exporting for checking: confirm the conditions have not changed and click Export CSV. If a "Query settings have changed" notice is shown, click Query first, otherwise the export button is grey.
5. Verifying history analysis: select no more than 20 tags over no more than 24 hours; after querying, the history analysis table appears below. Check Coverage and Good / samples to judge whether the data is trustworthy.

■ Good to know and common issues
1. Fewer curve details or incomplete Boolean transitions: over large ranges the system aggregates or downsamples, and Boolean tags show the sample mean, so fractions do not represent real intermediate states. Use a 1-hour or 6-hour range to inspect raw changes.
2. If the curves do not change after editing tags or time, the page says "Query settings have changed. The previous result is still displayed."; click Query to update. Export is also disabled meanwhile, so the exported data cannot differ from the conditions.
3. "Choose a valid time range with the end after the start" means the start and end are reversed or incomplete; select the times again and query.
4. If the history analysis table is missing, it covers at most 20 tags within the last 24 hours; reduce the tags or range and query again.
5. A tag passed in the address may be reported as not existing or not accessible because it was deleted or the account lacks view permission; select the required tag again in tag selection.
trends.summary: Turn history into curves so you can see when a value changed and what it changed to.
